**Q2.** A researcher claims: "Our LLM achieves 91.3% accuracy on the MedQA benchmark, outperforming the previous state of the art (89.7%) by 1.6 percentage points. This proves our model has superior medical knowledge."

Identify all the statistical concerns with this claim.

**Answer:**

**Concern 1 鈥?Statistical significance not established** : MedQA contains 1273 test questions. At 91.3% accuracy, the standard error is approximately 0.913脳0.087/1273鈮?.008\sqrt{0.913 \times 0.087 / 1273} \approx 0.0080.913脳0.087/1273鈥嬧増0.008 (0.8%). The 95% CI for accuracy is approximately 91.3%卤1.6%91.3\% \pm 1.6\%91.3%卤1.6%, ranging from 89.7% to 92.9%. The improvement of 1.6 percentage points is approximately at the boundary of statistical significance 鈥?the confidence intervals of the two models likely overlap substantially. The claim of "outperforming" is not clearly statistically supported.

**Concern 2 鈥?Multiple comparisons / look-elsewhere effect** : The "previous state of the art" of 89.7% was itself the best result from multiple prior attempts. The new claim of 91.3% reflects the best result from (presumably) multiple model variants and training configurations. The comparison conflates two best-of-many results without correcting for multiple comparisons. The true improvement over a truly fair single comparison could be zero.

**Concern 3 鈥?Benchmark contamination** : MedQA questions are publicly available. If the new model was trained on internet data containing these questions, or trained on any dataset derived from the same source (USMLE questions), the 91.3% may partly reflect training data memorization rather than genuine medical reasoning.

**Concern 4 鈥?The inference "superior medical knowledge"** : Benchmark accuracy measures performance on a specific set of multiple-choice questions. It does not measure: calibration (are the model's confidence levels reliable?), clinical reasoning quality on open-ended cases, performance on rare or novel conditions, robustness to distribution shift (different hospitals, different question phrasings), or safety (will the model give dangerous advice in edge cases?). "Superior medical knowledge" implies a broad capability claim; a single benchmark accuracy supports only a narrow task-specific claim.

**Concern 5 鈥?No uncertainty quantification** : The model achieves 91.3% 鈥?but how does it perform on questions it gets wrong? Does it express uncertainty on hard cases, or does it hallucinate confident wrong answers? For medical applications, calibration and uncertainty quantification (Section 21.3) matter as much as accuracy.

A more careful claim: "On the MedQA test set, our model achieves 91.3% accuracy (95% CI: 89.7%鈥?2.9%), compared to the previously reported best of 89.7%. This improvement, while statistically marginal and potentially confounded by benchmark contamination, warrants further evaluation on held-out clinical question sets with calibration assessment."

#### Think Deeper

**Q2.** A medical AI system uses conformal prediction (calibrated on 2,000 patients at a teaching hospital) to produce prediction sets for diagnosis classification. The system is deployed at a rural clinic serving a very different demographic population.

(a) What specific assumption does conformal prediction's coverage guarantee require? Is this assumption met in this deployment scenario? (b) If the calibration set under-represents elderly patients (5% elderly in calibration vs. 35% elderly at the rural clinic), describe specifically how the prediction sets might behave differently for elderly patients. (c) A radiologist argues: "If the coverage guarantee is invalid, the conformal prediction sets are useless. We should just use the model's raw probabilities." Evaluate this argument. (d) Propose a modification to the conformal prediction approach that would be more appropriate for this deployment context.

**Answer:**

**(a) Required assumption** : Conformal prediction's coverage guarantee requires **exchangeability** 鈥?the calibration examples and test examples are drawn from the same distribution (or more precisely, the full set of calibration + test examples is exchangeable, meaning any permutation is equally likely). This is approximately satisfied when calibration and test data come from the same population.

In this deployment scenario: **the assumption is not met**. The calibration data comes from a teaching hospital population, while the test data comes from a rural clinic with very different demographics, disease prevalence, case mix, and possibly different imaging equipment and scanning protocols. The non-conformity scores derived from the teaching hospital population will not correctly characterize how "surprising" errors are for rural clinic patients.

**(b) Behavior for elderly patients** : If elderly patients are underrepresented in calibration (5% of calibration vs. 35% of deployment), the non-conformity score quantile q^1鈭捨盶hat{q}_{1-\alpha}q^鈥?鈭捨扁€?was computed from a distribution where most patients are non-elderly. If the model makes systematically different errors for elderly patients (perhaps confidence is more diffuse for elderly patients with atypical presentations), the q^1鈭捨盶hat{q}_{1-\alpha}q^鈥?鈭捨扁€?threshold may be miscalibrated.

Two specific behaviors: (1) **Over-coverage for elderly** : if the model is less confident for elderly patients, their non-conformity scores are higher, and the calibration quantile (computed on non-elderly patients) may set a threshold that is too low 鈥?elderly patients' prediction sets are too large, generating too many diagnoses. (2) **Under-coverage for elderly** : if the model happens to be less accurate for elderly patients' common conditions (e.g., atypical presentations of pneumonia in elderly patients), the calibration threshold may not correctly capture the error rate 鈥?prediction sets may appear confident but exclude the true diagnosis more often than 伪\alpha伪 among elderly patients. Without stratified calibration, we cannot know which applies without empirical testing.

**(c) Evaluating the radiologist's argument** : The argument has a valid premise but an invalid conclusion.

**Valid premise** : The coverage guarantee does not hold in this distribution shift scenario, so the claim "this set contains the true diagnosis with 90% probability" cannot be trusted at face value.

**Invalid conclusion** : Raw probabilities are not better. Raw probabilities from the model are also miscalibrated for the new population 鈥?they were trained and/or calibrated on the teaching hospital distribution. A model that says "87% probability of pneumonia" for a rural clinic patient is making a claim its training distribution does not support.

The correct conclusion: both the conformal sets and the raw probabilities are suspect under distribution shift, for the same underlying reason. Conformal prediction is not uniquely deficient 鈥?it is simply more explicit about its assumptions. The practical guidance: either (1) recalibrate conformal prediction on a relevant sample from the deployment population, or (2) monitor the actual coverage empirically on cases where the true diagnosis becomes known, and adjust the q^\hat{q}q^鈥?threshold based on observed coverage.

**(d) Modification for this context** : **Stratified conformal prediction** or **local conformal prediction**.

In stratified conformal: maintain separate calibration sets for clinically relevant subgroups (elderly vs. non-elderly; or by primary presenting symptom; or by imaging equipment type). Compute separate non-conformity score quantiles for each stratum. At deployment, use the quantile corresponding to the patient's stratum to construct the prediction set. This provides correct coverage within each stratum if the deployment distribution matches the calibration distribution within strata.

Practically: collect even a small calibration set at the rural clinic itself (100鈥?00 patients with known diagnoses), compute local non-conformity scores, and supplement the teaching hospital calibration data. The local coverage guarantee will be more reliable for the actual deployment distribution than the teaching hospital calibration alone. This is an instance of domain adaptation 鈥?using target domain data to re-calibrate a source-domain model.

* * *

**Q1.** Consider the statement: "AI systems will eventually be able to do everything a statistician does, just faster."

Evaluate this claim using the statistical framework developed throughout this book. What would such a system need to be able to do that current AI systems cannot? Is the claim plausible? What irreducible human role, if any, remains?

**Discussion:**

This claim merits a careful statistical evaluation rather than a blanket acceptance or rejection.

**What current AI can do (impressively)** : AI systems can compute any statistical test, fit any model, generate visualizations, write and debug statistical code, summarize literature, and explain statistical concepts 鈥?all faster than most humans. For many routine statistical analyses, an AI system can already produce competent work given a well-specified problem.

**What statistical reasoning actually requires, beyond computation** :

_Question formulation_ : Deciding what to measure, what population to study, what counts as the outcome. This requires understanding the decision that statistics is supposed to support 鈥?which requires domain knowledge, stakeholder engagement, and value judgments that are not derivable from data. An AI trained on past statistical practice can generate plausible question framings, but whether a question is the right one to ask is a human judgment.

_Causal assumption auditing_ : Drawing a DAG requires knowing what might plausibly cause what 鈥?domain knowledge that goes beyond text patterns. Deciding whether the parallel trends assumption holds in a DiD design requires understanding the mechanisms that might violate it. A language model that generates causal graphs is producing text patterns that look like causal graphs; it is not performing causal reasoning.

_Ethical judgment_ : Choosing between fairness definitions (Chapter 20), deciding what counts as practically significant, determining when to share interim results 鈥?these are value-laden choices. AI systems can describe the choices and their tradeoffs; they cannot make them on behalf of affected communities.

_Knowing when the data cannot answer the question_ : Recognizing that the available data cannot identify the causal effect of interest (because there is no valid instrument, no exogenous variation, no experimental control) is a form of epistemic humility that requires understanding what statistical methods require and what they can provide. A system optimized to always generate an answer may systematically fail at this.

**A calibrated conclusion** : The claim "AI will eventually do everything a statistician does" may be true for the _computational_ parts of statistics. The irreducible human contributions are those that require: (1) defining what question is worth answering, (2) making value-laden choices that affect which stakeholders are served, (3) taking responsibility for the conclusions and their implications.

Statistical thinking is the art of reasoning carefully under uncertainty in service of decisions. The reasoning itself can be augmented enormously by AI. The service 鈥?understanding whose decisions are being supported, what those decisions mean, and what it means to reason responsibly 鈥?remains irreducibly human.

### Chapter Summary

Language models are autoregressive probabilistic models that generate text by sampling from a learned conditional distribution over next tokens. This framing explains hallucination precisely: for frequently-seen patterns, the distribution is concentrated and sampling is reliable; for rare patterns, the distribution is diffuse and samples may be wrong 鈥?but the generated text looks identical either way.

**Temperature** and **top-p** are statistical knobs controlling sampling distribution spread. Low temperature reduces variance at the cost of diversity; high temperature increases creativity at the cost of reliability.

**Uncertainty quantification** is the critical gap in current AI systems. Standard models produce point predictions without uncertainty estimates. The solutions range from full **Bayesian neural networks** (principled but computationally expensive) to **conformal prediction** (rigorous frequentist coverage guarantees without modeling assumptions) to simple post-hoc **calibration** (at minimum, ensuring probabilities match observed frequencies).

**Conformal prediction** provides the cleanest rigorous solution: prediction sets with guaranteed coverage (P(true label鈭圕(x))鈮?鈭捨盤(\text{true label} \in C(x)) \geq 1-\alphaP(true label鈭圕(x))鈮?鈭捨? derived from held-out calibration data, without assumptions on model architecture.

**Benchmark gaming and the look-elsewhere effect** (Thread B) apply to AI evaluation as they apply to scientific publication: benchmark scores are inflated by multiple comparisons across the field, possible test set contamination, and publication bias toward impressive results.

Thread C concludes: a large language model performs posterior predictive sampling 鈥?statistically sophisticated, computationally extraordinary, and bounded by precisely what statistical theory says it must be bounded by. The irreplaceable human contributions are question formulation, causal reasoning, ethical judgment, and epistemic humility about what the data cannot answer.

In the next chapter, we ask how to use AI well in statistical work 鈥?not replacing statistical judgment, but amplifying it.

## Chapter 22: AI as a Statistical Tool

There is a telling moment that happens in data science teams around the world when a new AI coding assistant arrives. A junior analyst, stuck on how to run a Cox proportional hazards model in R, asks the AI. Within seconds, the AI produces working code, explains what each argument does, and even notes a common pitfall with the baseline hazard estimate. The analyst is delighted. The analysis that would have taken an afternoon takes fifteen minutes.

Then the analyst runs the model on the wrong data.

Not because the AI made an error. The AI did exactly what was asked. But the analyst was analyzing time-to-event data from a clinical trial where the treatment was administered at varying times after enrollment 鈥?a complex situation where naively running a Cox model without accounting for the time-varying exposure gives biased estimates. The AI produced correct code for the question asked. The analyst asked the wrong question.

This scenario is not a cautionary tale about AI. It is a cautionary tale about statistical thinking 鈥?and about what statistical thinking actually is, as opposed to what the software can do. The AI is an extraordinary accelerant of the _computational_ parts of statistical work. But the parts that actually make statistical work valuable 鈥?deciding what question to ask, what data to use, what assumptions are justified, how to interpret the results 鈥?remain as demanding as ever.

This chapter is about using AI well in statistical work. Well means: exploiting AI's extraordinary capabilities while maintaining the human statistical judgment that makes the capabilities worth having.

### 22.1 Where AI Genuinely Helps

Let us be specific about what AI systems can do well, so we can calibrate our expectations precisely.

#### Exploratory Data Analysis

Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the process of understanding a dataset before formal modeling 鈥?checking distributions, finding missing values, identifying outliers, discovering patterns, generating hypotheses.

AI systems are excellent at EDA assistance:

* **Generating code for summaries** : Given a description of the dataset, an AI can produce comprehensive summary code (histograms, correlation matrices, missing value maps, outlier checks) in seconds.
* **Interpreting output** : An analyst who is new to a domain can show an AI their EDA output and receive sensible interpretations of what the patterns might mean.
* **Suggesting follow-up analyses** : Based on EDA findings, AI can suggest further checks 鈥?"your response variable appears right-skewed; consider examining whether a log transformation is appropriate" or "these two predictors have correlation 0.93 鈥?check for multicollinearity in your regression."

The important caveat: AI suggestions in EDA are pattern-matching against a vast corpus of statistical practice. They are heuristics, not theorems. The human statistician must evaluate whether the suggested analysis is appropriate for the _specific_ problem at hand 鈥?its measurement process, its design, its intended inference.

#### Code Generation and Debugging

This is perhaps AI's most immediately valuable capability for statistical work:

* **Translating method to code** : "Write me a power analysis for a two-sample t-test with effect size 0.4, alpha 0.05, and power 0.80" 鈫?correct R or Python code, faster than looking up the `pwr` package syntax.
* **Debugging** : Paste an error message and the code that generated it; AI identifies the issue and suggests fixes 鈥?often correctly, for common errors.
* **Translation between languages** : Convert R code to Python, Python to Stan, SQL to pandas 鈥?AI handles these mechanical translations well.

The caveat is the same as always: the AI produces code for the question it was asked. If the question was imprecisely specified, the code will answer the imprecise question. Verifying that the code answers the _intended_ question requires statistical judgment that the human must supply.

#### Literature Synthesis

Synthesizing a large body of scientific literature 鈥?identifying main findings, tracking evolving consensus, noting contradictions between studies 鈥?is time-consuming and error-prone when done manually. AI can assist by:

* Summarizing abstracts and key findings across many papers
* Identifying common methodological approaches in a literature
* Flagging contradictions between studies for closer examination
* Suggesting related literatures the analyst may have overlooked

The critical limitation: AI can misrepresent, confabulate, or miss key papers. Hallucination (Chapter 21) is particularly dangerous in literature synthesis because wrong citations look exactly like correct citations. Every factual claim about the literature must be verified against actual papers. Use AI for navigation; verify the map.

#### Assumption Documentation and Communication

AI can help draft documentation of statistical assumptions 鈥?which is frequently underdone in practice. Given a description of an analysis, AI can produce:

* A list of the statistical assumptions being made
* Plain-language explanations of what each assumption means
* Descriptions of what would happen if each assumption were violated
* Suggestions for sensitivity analyses

This is genuinely valuable. Written, explicit assumptions are the institutional memory that allows an analysis to be reviewed, critiqued, and improved. AI can generate a first draft of this documentation faster than a human, which increases the probability that it gets written at all.

### 22.2 The Limits That Cannot Be Automated

Now we turn to what AI cannot do in statistical work 鈥?and, critically, why these limits are not engineering failures waiting to be fixed, but fundamental constraints that arise from what statistical work _is_.

#### Question Formulation: What Are We Actually Trying to Know?

In Chapter 1, we distinguished between descriptive questions ("how many patients died?"), predictive questions ("who will die?"), and causal questions ("would this drug reduce mortality?"). These require fundamentally different analyses, data, and designs.

AI cannot determine which type of question is appropriate for a given decision. This requires:

* **Understanding the decision context** : Who will act on this analysis? What action are they considering? What would they do differently depending on the result?
* **Domain expertise** : What is known about the biological mechanisms, policy levers, or business processes involved?
* **Stakeholder engagement** : Whose interests are being served? Whose are at risk? What do they need to know?

An AI will answer the question you ask. If you ask "is X associated with Y?" it will run a correlation or regression. If you ask "does X cause Y?" it will describe methods for causal inference. But it cannot tell you which question you should have asked 鈥?because that requires understanding the decision that motivated the analysis.

The Cox model error in this chapter's opening is a question formulation failure. The analyst asked "what is the hazard ratio for treatment?" when they should have asked "given the time-varying nature of treatment assignment, what is the appropriate model for the causal effect of treatment on survival?"

#### Assumption Auditing: Are These Assumptions Actually Justified?

Every statistical method rests on assumptions. AI can list the assumptions of the Cox proportional hazards model: proportional hazards, independent censoring, no unmeasured confounders (if making causal claims), correct functional form. What AI cannot do is evaluate whether these assumptions hold _in your specific study_.

Is the proportional hazards assumption plausible for this treatment, given what is known about its mechanism of action? Is censoring plausibly independent, or might patients who withdrew from the study be systematically different from those who completed it? These questions require domain knowledge and judgment that AI does not have.

The analyst who asks AI "are my assumptions valid?" will receive a generic checklist. The analyst who says "my drug affects the baseline hazard function in ways I know about" and asks AI "given this, what does that imply for my Cox model?" will get a useful, substantive response. The human must supply the domain knowledge; AI helps reason about its implications.

#### Causal Reasoning: What Would Happen If We Intervened?

We spent Chapter 18 establishing that causal inference requires assumptions 鈥?about which variables are confounders, which are mediators, which are colliders 鈥?that the data alone cannot provide. These assumptions are a causal model of the world.

AI can help draw DAGs, compute the implications of causal assumptions, and run causal analyses once a causal structure is specified. It cannot specify the causal structure. Specifying the causal structure requires:

* Knowledge of the generating mechanisms (what causes what in this domain)
* Understanding of the data collection process (what variables were measured, how, and when)
* Engagement with the scientific or policy literature (what do domain experts believe)

Recall Chapter 18's closing warning: "The AI found it in the data" is not evidence of causation. This applies to AI-assisted statistical analysis: an AI that finds a strong association in observational data is not finding a cause. The human must decide whether the conditions for causal inference are met.

#### Result Interpretation: What Does This Mean for the Decision?

A regression model produces coefficient estimates, standard errors, and p-values. An AI can explain what each of these means statistically. What it cannot do is explain what they mean _for this decision, in this context, for these stakeholders_.

A coefficient of 0.15 on a marketing spend variable could mean: spend more, but only if you have reason to believe the regression controls for all relevant confounders; or do not spend more until you run an RCT; or the effect is statistically real but practically too small to be worth the cost. Which interpretation is correct depends on the decision context, the quality of the data, and the precision of the estimate 鈥?all of which require human judgment.

**Thread A's closing example** : A clinical trial shows that a new medication reduces blood pressure by 3 mmHg (95% CI: 1鈥? mmHg, p = 0.003). Is this clinically meaningful? An AI can tell you the definition of clinical significance and note that guidelines typically consider a threshold of X mmHg. It cannot weigh the drug's side effect profile, cost, patient preferences, and alternative treatments against this effect size 鈥?the full cost-benefit calculus that a physician and patient must perform together.

#### Ethical Judgment: What Should We Do With This Analysis?

Statistical analysis exists to support decisions. Decisions have ethical dimensions. When an analysis has implications for who gets resources, who bears risk, or whose rights are protected, statistical choices become ethical choices.

We saw in Chapter 20 that the choice between fairness definitions (equalized odds, demographic parity, calibration) is an ethical and political choice, not a technical one. AI cannot make this choice. It can describe the tradeoffs 鈥?and should be used for exactly that 鈥?but the decision must involve the affected communities.

Similarly: a data scientist working for a pharmaceutical company analyzing a clinical trial is not just performing statistics. They are participating in a process that will affect whether patients have access to an effective treatment, at what price, with what understanding of its risks. How to present results honestly 鈥?what to disclose, what to emphasize 鈥?requires integrity that is a human responsibility.

### 22.3 Thread C Conclusion: Amplification, Not Replacement

Thread C began in Chapter 1 with the observation that AI had automated computation but not judgment. We have now traced this thread through twenty-one chapters, accumulating evidence for a precise claim.

**AI amplifies statistical thinking. It does not replace it.**

The amplification is real and substantial. A statistician using AI tools can:

* Conduct EDA in minutes instead of hours
* Write and debug code in hours instead of days
* Synthesize literature in hours instead of weeks
* Generate thorough documentation and assumption lists effortlessly
* Explore many more model specifications in a given time budget

All of this is genuinely valuable. The time saved can be reinvested in the parts that require human judgment 鈥?asking better questions, engaging more deeply with domain experts, thinking more carefully about causal structure, communicating results more thoroughly.

The replacement claim is false. AI cannot formulate the right question, audit whether assumptions are justified in context, reason causally about interventions, interpret results in the decision context, or make the ethical judgments that responsible statistical work requires.

This is not a temporary limitation of current AI technology. It reflects what statistical work _is_ : reasoning under uncertainty in service of human decisions. The "in service of human decisions" part is irreducibly human. Decisions are made by humans, affect humans, and must be accountable to humans.

**Thread B's closing remark** : The replication crisis (Chapters 9, 10, 13, 18, 21) was a crisis of statistical practice 鈥?of researchers who had the computational tools to run analyses but did not always have the judgment to run them well. AI that makes analysis computationally easier could either exacerbate this crisis (by making it easier to run more analyses without thinking carefully about them) or ameliorate it (by making it easier to document assumptions, run sensitivity analyses, and pre-register). Which happens depends on the statistical culture we build 鈥?not on the AI tools themselves.

**Thread A's closing remark** : Through twenty-two chapters, we have followed medical diagnosis from Semmelweis's handwashing hypothesis (Chapter 1), through Bayes' theorem and mammography base rates (Chapter 3), through clinical trial design (Chapter 8), through confounders in observational data (Chapters 15, 18), through AI diagnostic evaluation (Chapter 20). The full picture: medical AI can be an extraordinary tool when deployed with rigorous statistical evaluation, honest communication of uncertainty, appropriate calibration, and clear-eyed acknowledgment of what observational data can and cannot establish about causation. AI without statistical judgment is a powerful tool pointed in an unknown direction.

### 22.4 A Framework for Human-AI Statistical Collaboration

Given the above, here is a practical framework for using AI well in statistical work.

**Step 1: Human defines the question.** Before turning to AI, the human statistician (in dialogue with domain experts and stakeholders) specifies: What decision does this analysis support? What causal or descriptive question does it ask? What data is available and what are its limitations?

**Step 2: Human articulates the causal model.** For any analysis with causal implications: draw a DAG (or describe the causal structure in words). Identify potential confounders, mediators, and instruments. Decide what assumptions are required and whether they are plausible.

**Step 3: AI assists with computation and code.** Given a well-specified question and causal model, AI generates the code to execute the analysis. Human reviews the code to verify it executes the intended analysis.

**Step 4: Human interprets results in context.** The AI can summarize what the numbers mean statistically. The human interprets what they mean for the decision, given the quality of the data, the plausibility of the assumptions, and the needs of the stakeholders.

**Step 5: Human communicates results.** Communicate effect sizes with confidence intervals (not just p-values). State assumptions explicitly. Distinguish statistical from practical significance. Describe what would change the conclusion. AI can draft this communication; the human verifies its accuracy and completeness.

**Step 6: Both human and AI check for common errors.** AI is excellent at checking for mechanical errors: wrong degrees of freedom, inappropriate tests for the data type, failure to account for multiple comparisons. Human checks for conceptual errors: wrong question, unjustified assumptions, misinterpreted results.

This is not "AI does the statistics, human checks the AI." It is "human does the statistics, AI handles the computation." The difference matters. The human remains the statistician; AI is the extraordinarily capable calculator.

### 22.5 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Describe three tasks in a statistical analysis where AI assistance is most valuable, and three tasks where human judgment cannot be delegated to AI. Explain briefly why each falls in its category.

**Answer:**

**Most valuable AI assistance** :

  1. **Code generation for standard methods** : Given a precisely specified statistical procedure, AI produces correct, working code faster than manual lookup of syntax. This is low-risk because the code can be verified by running it.

  2. **EDA code and output summarization** : AI can quickly generate comprehensive data summaries (distributions, missing values, correlations) and interpret what patterns might mean 鈥?providing a starting checklist the human analyst can evaluate and extend.

  3. **Documentation of statistical assumptions** : AI can produce a first draft of a complete assumptions document (what each method assumes, what violations would imply) faster than manual writing, improving the probability that assumptions are documented at all.

**Human judgment irreplaceable** :

  1. **Question formulation** : Deciding whether the appropriate question is descriptive, predictive, or causal 鈥?and what data and design can answer it 鈥?requires understanding the decision context, domain knowledge, and stakeholder needs that AI lacks.

  2. **Causal structure specification** : Drawing a DAG and deciding which variables are confounders, mediators, and colliders requires domain expertise about mechanisms. AI can help reason about a specified DAG; it cannot specify the DAG from domain knowledge it does not have.

  3. **Ethical and practical interpretation of results** : Deciding what a statistically significant result means for a real decision 鈥?whether a 3 mmHg blood pressure reduction justifies the cost and side effects of a new drug 鈥?requires weighing values and context that are irreducibly human.

* * *

**Q2.** A colleague uses AI to run an observational analysis of whether remote work reduces employee burnout. The AI: (a) cleaned the data, (b) ran a regression of burnout on remote work status controlling for job type and tenure, (c) found a significant negative coefficient (more remote work 鈫?lower burnout, p = 0.002), (d) concluded "remote work reduces burnout."

Identify at least three statistical concerns that the AI-assisted analysis may have missed.

**Answer:**

**Concern 1 鈥?Confounders not controlled** : The regression controls for job type and tenure but likely misses important confounders. Employees who work remotely may also have more autonomy, more flexible hours, better management, higher job satisfaction independent of remote work, or simply different personality types (introverts who chose jobs enabling remote work). Job type and tenure are not sufficient to control for all of these. Without a causal structure justification (a DAG showing that job type and tenure block all backdoor paths), the coefficient cannot be causally interpreted.

**Concern 2 鈥?Self-selection / reverse causation** : Who chooses to work remotely (in a company where it is optional) may be systematically different from those who do not. Employees with lower burnout may be better positioned to negotiate remote work arrangements. If burnout affects remote work status (reverse causation) as well as remote work affecting burnout, ordinary regression does not identify the causal direction.

**Concern 3 鈥?Measurement of burnout** : How is burnout measured? A self-report survey answered by current employees may suffer from survivorship bias (highly burned-out employees may have already quit, leaving lower-burnout people in the sample). The regression may be showing "remote workers who are still employed have lower burnout than in-person workers who are still employed" 鈥?not "remote work prevents burnout."

**Concern 4 鈥?Multiple comparisons** : If the analyst (with or without AI) ran several model specifications (different covariates, different burnout measures, different subsets) and reported the most significant result, the p = 0.002 may be inflated by multiple comparisons. Pre-registration or Bonferroni correction would be needed.

**Concern 5 鈥?Ecological vs. individual inference** : If the analysis uses aggregate data (department-level burnout averages vs department-level remote work rates), regression coefficients describe department-level associations and cannot be extrapolated to individual-level causal effects.

**Conclusion** : The AI competently ran the requested regression. The problems are in what was asked: a causal conclusion from an observational analysis without a credible causal identification strategy. "AI said p = 0.002" is not statistical evidence of causation.

**Q3.** An AI assistant produces the following output for an analyst who asks: "Analyze my dataset and tell me what's driving customer churn." The AI produces a table of feature importances from a gradient-boosted model, identifies the top predictor as "days since last login," and concludes: "Customers who haven't logged in for 30+ days are the main driver of churn. You should target them with re-engagement campaigns."

Identify what the AI did well, what it did poorly, and what critical questions a human statistician would ask that the AI did not.

**Answer:**

**What the AI did well** : The AI competently executed a well-defined computational task 鈥?it fit a model, computed feature importances, and produced a clear output. Generating a gradient-boosted model and extracting feature importances is exactly the kind of mechanical statistical computation that AI handles well. The recommendation ("re-engagement campaigns") is actionable and follows directly from the model output.

**What the AI did poorly** :

_Causation vs. correlation_ : "Days since last login" predicts churn, but is this causal? Customers who are dissatisfied may reduce login frequency and then churn 鈥?low login days is a symptom, not a cause. Targeting customers with low login days for re-engagement campaigns will target customers who are already in the process of churning, not necessarily address the underlying dissatisfaction that caused both low logins and eventual churn. The model found a strong predictor; the AI concluded it was a lever without asking whether it is one.

_Wrong question_ : "What drives churn?" is ambiguous. The AI interpreted it as "what predicts churn best in a model?" A human analyst would first ask: "What is the decision we're trying to support? Are we trying to predict who will churn (for retention resource allocation), understand why they churn (for product improvement), or test an intervention (for a randomized trial of re-engagement)?" These require different analyses.

_No uncertainty quantification_ : The AI reported feature importances as facts without confidence intervals or model uncertainty. How stable are these importances across cross-validation folds? Is "days since last login" reliably the top feature or is it tied with others?

**Critical questions a human would ask** :

  1. Is this association stable across time periods and customer cohorts, or does the model overfit to a specific period?
  2. What is the counterfactual? If we send re-engagement emails to at-risk customers, what fraction respond, and does it reduce churn 鈥?or is the "at-risk" signal already too late?
  3. What is the feature engineering for "days since last login"? Is this measured at the right time relative to the churn decision?
  4. Are there important subgroups where the driver differs (e.g., enterprise vs. consumer customers)?

* * *

**Q4.** This chapter describes a framework where "the human does the statistics, AI handles the computation." What does this framework imply about the training and skills a statistical analyst needs in an age where AI can generate code, suggest models, and interpret results?

**Answer:**

The framework implies that the _most valuable_ skills shift upward in abstraction 鈥?away from mechanical competencies and toward judgment competencies.

**Skills that become less essential** (AI handles these well):

* Writing code from scratch for standard statistical methods
* Memorizing software syntax for specific packages
* Performing basic arithmetic calculations in analysis
* Producing standard visualizations and summary tables

**Skills that become more essential** :

_Question formulation_ : The ability to translate a business or scientific problem into a precise statistical question 鈥?deciding whether it is descriptive, predictive, or causal; identifying what data would answer it; recognizing when it cannot be answered with available data. AI can respond to stated questions but cannot evaluate whether you asked the right question.

_Causal reasoning_ : Specifying DAGs, identifying confounders vs. mediators vs. colliders, evaluating whether identification assumptions are plausible in a specific domain. AI can implement causal analyses when given a specified causal structure but cannot provide the domain knowledge to justify that structure.

_Critical evaluation_ : Reading AI-generated code and results critically enough to detect when the AI answered a different question than intended, used an inappropriate method, or produced a subtly wrong analysis. This requires understanding what the methods do, not just how to run them.

_Uncertainty communication_ : Translating statistical results into honest, contextually appropriate communication for non-statistical audiences 鈥?not just what the numbers say, but what they mean for the decision, what their limitations are, and what should not be concluded.

_Ethical judgment_ : Recognizing when an analysis has fairness, equity, or ethical implications that require human decision-making, not algorithmic optimization.

The practical implication: statistical education should increasingly emphasize conceptual understanding (why does this method work? when does it fail?) over mechanical proficiency (how do I code this?), and should explicitly train critical AI output evaluation as a core competency.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** You are a data scientist helping a team build an AI system to predict hospital readmission. The team presents you with a model achieving 0.81 AUC on the validation set and asks: "Can we deploy this?"

Using the framework from this book, design a complete pre-deployment evaluation plan. What questions must be answered before deployment? What analyses would you run?

Hint

Think about: calibration, fairness, subgroup performance, the actual decision this model will support, and what happens when the model is wrong.

**Answer:** A complete pre-deployment evaluation plan:

**Question 1: What decision does this model support?**

First, clarify the deployment use case: Is the model used to trigger nurse follow-up calls? Allocate care coordination resources? Route patients to intensive discharge planning? The decision determines which errors are most costly (false negatives that miss high-risk patients vs. false positives that waste resources on low-risk patients), which informs the choice of operating threshold and the metrics to prioritize.

**Question 2: Is the model well-calibrated?**

AUC = 0.81 measures discrimination (ranking) but not calibration. Construct a reliability diagram: group predicted probabilities into deciles and compare mean predicted probability to observed readmission rate in each decile. Compute ECE. If the model predicts "70% readmission risk," do 70% of those patients actually readmit? If not, any downstream resource allocation based on predicted probabilities is based on miscalibrated numbers.

**Question 3: What is the confusion matrix at the intended operating threshold?**

The operating threshold must be chosen based on the decision context. If each high-risk patient receives a care coordinator call at 200 USD, and the benefit of preventing a readmission is estimated at 10,000 USD, then the cost-benefit suggests a threshold where expected benefit > cost. Compute sensitivity, specificity, precision at this threshold. How many false positives? How many missed readmissions?

**Question 4: Is the model fair across patient subgroups?**

Run subgroup analysis by age group, race/ethnicity, insurance status, primary diagnosis category, and hospital unit. For each subgroup, report:

* Accuracy (and compare to overall)
* AUC (does discrimination hold up?)
* Calibration (are predicted risks equally calibrated across groups?)
* False positive rate and false negative rate (equalized odds)

Document any significant subgroup differences and their potential impact. A model that performs well overall but poorly for a minority subgroup will systematically under-serve those patients.

**Question 5: Is there data leakage?**

Review the feature list with a timestamp audit. Verify that every feature reflects information available _before_ the readmission decision (ideally, before or at discharge). If any feature could only be documented after readmission becomes known (e.g., any notation written post-discharge), remove it.

**Question 6: Does the model perform on the intended deployment distribution?**

The validation set should reflect the actual deployment population (same hospital system, same time period). If the model was trained at one hospital and will be deployed at another, evaluate on a held-out sample from the deployment hospital. Distribution shift is a major source of post-deployment performance degradation.

**Question 7: What is the plan for monitoring in deployment?**

Pre-deployment evaluation is a snapshot. Patient populations, treatment practices, and coding practices change over time. Design a monitoring plan: regularly compute model performance on new patients with known 30-day outcomes; trigger a re-evaluation if performance degrades significantly (use a statistical control chart for the AUC metric).

**Synthesis** : The 0.81 AUC is a promising starting point, not a deployment decision. Deployment should proceed only after completing a calibration analysis, a subgroup fairness audit, a data leakage audit, and validation on the deployment population 鈥?and only after establishing a monitoring plan.

* * *

**Q2.** The thread through this book has been "statistics is reasoning under uncertainty in service of human decisions." Reflect on the three threads 鈥?Thread A (Medical Diagnosis), Thread B (Replication Crisis), Thread C (AI and Statistics) 鈥?and write a synthesis paragraph explaining how they are unified by this theme.

**Answer:**

The three threads are three manifestations of the same fundamental challenge.

**Thread A** shows what happens when statistical reasoning is absent or incomplete in medicine. Semmelweis had the data but lacked the inferential framework to convince his colleagues. The base rate neglect in breast cancer screening leads to well-intentioned harm from unnecessary biopsies. Wakefield's fraudulent study, amplified by media and mistrusted institutions, caused preventable deaths from measles. And the promise of AI diagnostics, if evaluated without calibration, fairness, and causal thinking, repeats every error the thread documented 鈥?at scale.

**Thread B** shows what happens when scientists have the tools to compute but not the institutional or cultural structures to reason carefully under uncertainty. P-hacking, HARKing, publication bias, and garden-of-forking-paths created a body of "statistically significant" literature that largely failed to replicate. The reforms 鈥?pre-registration, open data, registered reports, transparent assumption documentation 鈥?are not technical innovations. They are commitments to honest reasoning under uncertainty: deciding what you will look for before you look, reporting what you found rather than what you wanted to find, and acknowledging what you cannot conclude from the data you have.

**Thread C** shows that AI, for all its computational power, inherits the limitations of the statistical framework it embodies. AI that hallucinates is a system that samples from a distribution without knowing when it is sampling from an uninformative region. AI that finds correlations but cannot establish causes is a system that has mastered rung 1 of Pearl's causal hierarchy but cannot climb to rung 2. AI evaluation that games benchmarks is a system evaluated under p-hacking-style incentives without pre-registration. The thread's conclusion is not pessimistic: AI amplifies what statistical reasoning can accomplish. But "amplifies" is different from "replaces." The reasoning 鈥?the careful thinking about what question to ask, what assumptions are justified, and what the results mean for a human decision 鈥?remains irreducibly human.

All three threads converge on a single lesson: **statistical tools are only as good as the judgment that deploys them.** The tools in this book 鈥?probability, Bayes' theorem, hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, regression, causal inference, Bayesian computation, model evaluation 鈥?are not algorithms for producing correct answers. They are frameworks for reasoning carefully under uncertainty. They require a human who cares about getting the right answer, who is honest about what the data can and cannot say, and who remembers that statistics exists in service of real decisions affecting real people.

#### Think Deeper

**Q2.** The book argues that AI amplifies statistical thinking but does not replace it. A critic responds: "This is just a defensive argument by statisticians protecting their jobs. In 10 years, AI will handle everything 鈥?including question formulation and causal reasoning 鈥?better than humans."

Steel-man this critic's argument (present the strongest version of it), then explain where you think the argument fails and why.

**Discussion:**

**Steel-manned argument** : The critic's strongest case rests on three observations.

First, _historical underestimation_ : humans have consistently underestimated AI capability advances, dismissing each previous frontier as "things AI can't do" until AI did them. Chess: impossible until Kasparov lost. Go: AI couldn't have sufficient intuition until AlphaGo crushed the world champion. "Genuine" language understanding: impossible until LLMs produced work indistinguishable from (and sometimes better than) humans in many domains. Question formulation sounds like a high-level human judgment 鈥?but AI systems have generated novel scientific hypotheses (AlphaFold predicted protein structures that changed biology), suggested experimental designs, and discovered patterns that led researchers to new questions. Treating "question formulation" as forever beyond AI may repeat the historical error of underestimation.

Second, _implicit vs. explicit reasoning_ : the claim that causal reasoning "requires domain knowledge AI doesn't have" may conflate the mechanism with the output. A sufficiently large model trained on all of scientific literature may implicitly learn the causal structures of many domains 鈥?not by reasoning in Pearl's framework but by learning which patterns of evidence and argument are associated with valid causal claims in each domain. The output might be indistinguishable from genuine causal reasoning without reproducing the explicit mechanism statisticians use.

Third, _AI-AI collaboration_ : even if individual AI systems cannot formulate causal questions today, a system of AI agents 鈥?one generating candidate questions, another evaluating them against domain constraints, another simulating potential confounders 鈥?might collectively produce outputs that match or exceed what a human statistician does.

**Where the argument fails** :

_Causal reasoning requires grounding in the world, not just text_ : Scientific causal knowledge is grounded in experimental evidence, physical mechanisms, and intervention experiences that extend beyond what any text corpus captures. AlphaFold succeeded at a problem 鈥?protein structure prediction 鈥?where the function is purely geometric and the criterion is purely structural. Causal inference requires understanding what would happen if we intervened in the world in a specific way. This is grounded in experiment, not text. A model that has never manipulated anything cannot reliably predict the consequences of manipulation.

_Value judgments cannot be delegated_ : The argument fails most clearly on the ethical components. Which fairness criterion to optimize, how to weigh Type I vs. Type II errors for a specific decision-maker, what counts as a "meaningful" effect 鈥?these require understanding whose interests are being served and what those people value. An AI that optimizes a specified criterion does not, in itself, determine what criterion to specify. The choice of criterion is irreducibly a human value judgment that requires understanding the affected parties.

_Accountability requires humans in the loop_ : Even if an AI system were epistemically equivalent to a statistician, legal and ethical accountability requires human judgment in high-stakes decisions. The question "who is responsible when the analysis is wrong?" cannot be answered by pointing to an algorithm. This is not a limitation of AI capability but a feature of how moral responsibility works among humans.

The conclusion is not "AI can never improve" but rather: the specifically human contributions to statistical work 鈥?value judgment, moral accountability, grounding in world experience 鈥?are not eliminated by better algorithms because they are not algorithmic problems in the first place.

* * *

**Q1.** We are entering a period where AI can produce competent statistical analyses from natural language descriptions of problems. A student who has not learned statistics can ask an AI to "run a regression on my data" and receive a working analysis. Does this change what statistical education should teach? Should statistics courses focus less on computation and more on something else 鈥?and if so, what?

**Discussion:**

This question is genuinely open, and statistical education is actively debating it. The discussion below represents several defensible positions.

**What AI changes** : If AI reliably generates correct code for any standard statistical procedure given a well-specified problem, then teaching students to write that code manually has reduced educational value. Students who can specify problems precisely and evaluate outputs critically may be better served than students who can write OLS from scratch.

**What AI does not change** : The intellectual core of statistical reasoning 鈥?understanding why a method is appropriate, what assumptions it requires, how to diagnose violations, how to interpret results causally rather than descriptively 鈥?is exactly what AI cannot replace, and therefore exactly what remains most valuable to teach.

**A possible reorganization of statistical education** :

_Less emphasis on_ : mechanical computation, formula memorization, and software syntax (AI handles these well). Rote hypothesis testing procedures applied to toy examples.

_More emphasis on_ : causal thinking and DAGs (the most important tool that AI cannot supply). Study design 鈥?randomization, blocking, power analysis, pre-registration (the institutional solutions to the replication crisis). Uncertainty communication 鈥?how to translate statistical results for non-statistical audiences, what confidence intervals mean for decisions. Critical evaluation of statistical claims 鈥?reading a paper and identifying whether the analysis justifies its conclusions, recognizing p-hacking and confounders.

_New emphasis on_ : AI output evaluation 鈥?recognizing when AI-generated code answers the wrong question; understanding what assumptions underlie AI-generated analyses; knowing when to distrust AI results.

The most valuable statistical education in the age of AI teaches students to reason carefully about causal questions, to design studies that produce valid evidence, to communicate uncertainty honestly, and to evaluate statistical claims critically 鈥?including AI-generated ones. These are precisely the skills that AI amplifies but cannot replace.

This is not an abandonment of quantitative training. Students must understand distributions, sampling, estimation, and inference deeply enough to evaluate whether an analysis makes sense. But the goal shifts from "can you compute this?" to "can you think about this?" 鈥?which is, arguably, what statistical education was always supposed to accomplish.

### Chapter Summary

AI is a powerful amplifier of statistical computation. It is not a replacement for statistical thinking.

**What AI does well** : code generation and debugging, EDA assistance, literature synthesis navigation, assumption documentation drafts, and mechanical error checking. These capabilities genuinely accelerate the computational parts of statistical work, freeing time for judgment.

**What AI cannot do** : formulate the right question, specify a causal model from domain knowledge, audit whether assumptions are justified in context, interpret results in the decision context, or make the ethical judgments that responsible analysis requires.

The **human-AI collaboration framework** maintains the human as the statistician: defining the question, specifying the causal structure, interpreting the results, and taking responsibility for the conclusions. AI handles the computation 鈥?extraordinarily well, and at extraordinary speed.

Thread A closes: from Semmelweis to modern AI diagnostics, the lesson is consistent. Statistical tools produce value when deployed with rigorous thinking about what question is being asked, what the data can support, and what the results mean for the people they affect.

Thread B closes: the replication crisis was a failure of statistical culture, not just statistical methods. The reforms 鈥?pre-registration, open science, honest uncertainty communication 鈥?are commitments to reasoning carefully under uncertainty in ways that survive review. AI makes computation easier; it does not automatically make the culture better.

Thread C closes: AI amplifies statistical thinking, does not replace it. The statistician's irreplaceable contributions are question formulation, causal reasoning, ethical judgment, and epistemic humility. AI handles the rest.

In the next chapter, we turn to experimental design 鈥?the set of decisions made _before_ data collection that determine whether any analysis is possible. Good statistics, like good architecture, begins with the blueprint.
