## Chapter 23: Experimental Design

An old statistician's joke goes like this: a farmer wants to know which fertilizer grows the biggest crops. He plants his best fields with the new fertilizer and his worst fields with the old one. After the harvest, the new fertilizer wins by a wide margin. The farmer is delighted. The statistician is not.

The joke lands because the error is obvious once you see it: the "best fields" would have outperformed the "worst fields" regardless of which fertilizer was used. The fertilizer comparison is confounded with field quality 鈥?a confounder so obvious that only someone who has never heard of experimental design would make the error.

But in real experiments, the equivalent errors are far less obvious. A clinical trial that enrolls patients by referral from specialist physicians enrolls sicker patients than one that advertises in a general newspaper. An online experiment that runs during the holiday season encounters different users than one run in March. A psychological study conducted in a university with voluntary participants does not study the general population. In each case, the design of the study 鈥?the decisions made before a single measurement is taken 鈥?determines whether the resulting analysis can say anything trustworthy.

This is the central lesson of experimental design: **statistics happens before you collect data, or it is too late.** No amount of analytical cleverness can recover a fundamentally flawed design. But a good design can make even simple analyses reliable and interpretable.

### 23.1 The Three Pillars of Experimental Design

Every well-designed experiment rests on three foundational principles. Together, they are what separates an experiment that can answer a causal question from one that produces association data.

#### Randomization

**Randomization** means assigning experimental units to treatment conditions by chance 鈥?not by convenience, preference, or any characteristic of the unit.

We established in Chapter 18 why randomization is the key to causal inference: it distributes all confounders 鈥?observed and unobserved 鈥?equally across treatment groups in expectation. The treated and control groups become comparable not because we measured and controlled for everything that might differ between them, but because chance equalizes them on everything, including what we did not think to measure.

Randomization does not eliminate variation. Some random samples will, by chance, have more sick patients in the treatment arm than the control arm. But because this imbalance is due to chance, statistical tests correctly account for it 鈥?the p-value tells us the probability of seeing this imbalance under the null hypothesis of no treatment effect.

Without randomization, there is always the worry: "The treatment group is different from the control group in some way we did not account for." With randomization, we can quantify exactly how different they might be due to chance, and any difference beyond that is attributable to the treatment.

**Practical randomization** : Use a true random number generator (not "alternating assignments" or "every other patient" 鈥?these can be predicted and gamed). For small studies, use stratified randomization (see below) to prevent chance imbalance on key variables.

#### Replication

**Replication** means applying each treatment to multiple experimental units 鈥?not just one.

If you apply fertilizer A to one field and fertilizer B to another, any difference in yield could be due to the fertilizer or to idiosyncratic features of those two fields (soil drainage, shading, water table depth). With one field per treatment, you cannot distinguish treatment effects from unit-level variation.

Replication allows you to estimate the variability within each treatment group. The standard error of the difference between treatment means 鈥?which determines the width of your confidence interval and the power of your test 鈥?is 蟽A2/nA+蟽B2/nB\sqrt{\sigma_A^2/n_A + \sigma_B^2/n_B}蟽A2鈥?nA鈥?蟽B2鈥?nB鈥嬧€? Without multiple units per group, 蟽\sigma蟽 is unknown and standard statistical inference is impossible.

The number of replications required is determined by **power analysis** (Section 23.3).

#### Control

**Control** means comparing the treated group to a meaningful baseline. Without a control, you cannot distinguish the effect of treatment from the passage of time, placebo effects, natural recovery, regression to the mean, or any other concurrent change.

The control group should be as similar as possible to the treatment group in everything except the treatment itself 鈥?which is why randomization and control go together.

In drug trials, the control is typically a placebo 鈥?a pill identical in appearance and taste to the active drug, but without the active ingredient. The placebo controls for the psychological effect of believing you are being treated. In blinded trials, neither the patient nor the physician knows who received placebo or treatment 鈥?preventing the physician's behavior from differing between groups.

### 23.2 Blocking: Reducing Noise Before You Start

Randomization guarantees that confounders are equalized _in expectation_ 鈥?on average, across many replications of the experiment. In any single experiment, chance can create imbalance. The more variable the experimental units, the more likely a chance imbalance could look like a treatment effect.

**Blocking** reduces this variability by grouping similar experimental units together before randomization, then randomizing within each group.

Return to the farmer. Suppose the fields differ in quality 鈥?some are naturally more fertile. Instead of randomizing all fields to fertilizer A or B, the farmer identifies pairs of adjacent fields with similar quality. Within each pair, one field is randomly assigned to A and the other to B. Each pair is a **block**.

The analysis then compares A vs. B within each block. Within-block comparisons are cleaner 鈥?the fields in each pair are as similar as possible except for the fertilizer. The variability due to field quality is controlled by design, not by statistical adjustment.

The general rule: **block what you can, randomize what you cannot.** Variables you can identify as major sources of variability should be used to form blocks. Variables you cannot identify or measure are handled by randomization.

In clinical trials, patients are often blocked by:

* **Gender** : randomize separately within male and female patients (equal representation guaranteed)
* **Disease severity** : randomize separately within severity strata
* **Clinical site** : randomize within each hospital in a multi-site trial (prevents the imbalance from chance over-enrollment of one site's patients)

#### Definition: Randomized Block Design

A **randomized block design** partitions experimental units into BBB blocks of similar units, then randomly assigns treatments within each block.

The statistical advantage: by removing block-to-block variability from the error term, the estimated treatment effect has a smaller standard error 鈥?which means greater precision with the same number of units, or the same precision with fewer units.

In plain language: blocking lets you "use up" known sources of variability, leaving a cleaner signal for the treatment effect.

### 23.3 Power Analysis: Designing for Success

One of the most consequential design decisions is sample size. Too small: you cannot detect a real effect (low power 鈥?high Type II error rate). Too large: you waste resources and may be unethical (exposing unnecessary patients to an experimental treatment when you could have answered the question with fewer).

**Power analysis** determines the sample size needed to achieve a desired probability of detecting an effect of a specified size.

Recall from Chapter 8: the four interconnected quantities in hypothesis testing are:

* **伪 \alpha伪** (Type I error rate): probability of rejecting the null when it is true (false positive rate)
* **尾 \beta尾** (Type II error rate): probability of failing to reject the null when it is false (false negative rate)
* **Power** (1鈭捨? - \beta1鈭捨?: probability of correctly detecting a real effect
* **Effect size 未\delta未**: the magnitude of the true difference to be detected
* **Sample size nnn**: what we solve for

Fixing 伪\alpha伪, power, and 未\delta未, the required sample size per arm for a two-sample t-test is:

n=(z1鈭捨?2+z1鈭捨?2鈰?蟽2未2n = \frac{(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^2 \cdot 2\sigma^2}{\delta^2}n=未2(z1鈭捨?2鈥?z1鈭捨测€?2鈰?蟽2鈥?
where 蟽2\sigma^2蟽2 is the within-group variance and 未\delta未 is the minimum effect size we want to detect.

At 伪=0.05\alpha = 0.05伪=0.05 (two-sided) and power = 0.80: z0.975=1.96z_{0.975} = 1.96z0.975鈥?1.96, z0.80=0.84z_{0.80} = 0.84z0.80鈥?0.84. So (z1鈭捨?2+z1鈭捨?2=(1.96+0.84)2=7.84(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^2 = (1.96 + 0.84)^2 = 7.84(z1鈭捨?2鈥?z1鈭捨测€?2=(1.96+0.84)2=7.84.

n鈮?.84鈰?蟽2未2=15.68蟽2未2n \approx \frac{7.84 \cdot 2\sigma^2}{\delta^2} = \frac{15.68 \sigma^2}{\delta^2}n鈮埼?7.84鈰?蟽2鈥?未215.68蟽2鈥?
**Choosing effect sizes** : The minimum detectable effect 未\delta未 should be the smallest effect that would be _practically meaningful_ , not the effect you expect to find. A drug that reduces blood pressure by 0.5 mmHg is statistically detectable with enough participants, but clinically meaningless. Power for a practically meaningful effect size prevents the "statistically significant but clinically irrelevant" outcome.

Cohen's conventions for standardized effect sizes (effect size divided by standard deviation) provide rough benchmarks: small = 0.2, medium = 0.5, large = 0.8. But domain-specific judgments should always take precedence over generic conventions.

#### Common Misconception

A common error is to use pilot study results to estimate the effect size for power analysis, then power the main study to detect that effect. This is circular: the pilot study's effect estimate is noisy (small sample), typically overestimates the true effect (winner's curse 鈥?small samples detect effects only when they happen to be large), and then the main study is powered to detect the inflated pilot estimate. The result: a main study with inflated power expectations that is underpowered in practice. Power analyses should be based on the minimum _clinically meaningful_ effect, not the estimated effect.

### 23.4 Factorial Designs: Testing Multiple Factors Efficiently

In many research questions, multiple factors affect the outcome. Studying them one at a time is inefficient 鈥?and misses interactions.

A **factorial design** simultaneously varies multiple factors across all combinations, allowing estimates of:

* The main effect of each factor (averaging over all levels of the other factors)
* The **interaction effect** : whether the effect of one factor depends on the level of another

**Example** : A company wants to test two website changes 鈥?a new headline (A vs. B) and a new button color (red vs. green). Instead of testing headline changes in one experiment and color changes in another, a 2脳22 \times 22脳2 factorial design tests all four combinations simultaneously:

| Button Red | Button Green  
---|---|---  
**Headline A** | 1000 users | 1000 users  
**Headline B** | 1000 users | 1000 users  
  
This design answers three questions with 4000 users:

  1. Does headline affect conversion? (Compare A vs. B, averaging over colors)
  2. Does button color affect conversion? (Compare red vs. green, averaging over headlines)
  3. Does the headline effect depend on button color? (Interaction)

Without factorial design, three separate two-arm experiments would require 6000 users to answer the same three questions 鈥?a 50% efficiency gain.

#### Interaction Effects

The interaction is often the most important finding. Suppose Headline B increases conversion dramatically when the button is green, but not when it is red. The main effect of headline (averaging over colors) would be moderate 鈥?missing the crucial fact that the headline only works in combination with the green button.

An **interaction** between factors A and B means: the effect of A depends on the level of B (or equivalently, the effect of B depends on the level of A). Factorial designs are the only way to detect interactions. Separate one-factor experiments, by definition, cannot.

### 23.5 Pre-Registration: The Institutional Fix for p-Hacking

We have discussed pre-registration in Chapters 9 (as the solution to the replication crisis) and 13 (as the frequentist analog to Bayesian's use of explicit priors). Here we can describe it in full as an experimental design tool.

**Pre-registration** means publicly committing to the study design, hypothesis, primary outcome measure, sample size, and analysis plan _before data collection begins_. The pre-registration is time-stamped and publicly accessible (e.g., on ClinicalTrials.gov for medical research, OSF.io for social science).

Pre-registration does not constrain what you observe. It constrains what you claim to have predicted. After the study, you may run any exploratory analyses you like 鈥?but you must clearly distinguish pre-registered confirmatory analyses from post-hoc exploratory ones.

**Why pre-registration works against p-hacking** :

p-hacking (Chapter 9) exploits the flexibility in the garden of forking paths: choosing the outcome measure, the covariates, the sample (who to exclude), and the statistical test _after seeing the data_ to achieve significance. Pre-registration eliminates this flexibility retrospectively by making the choices public before any data are seen.

A study with a pre-registered primary analysis has a genuine Type I error rate of 伪\alpha伪. A study with post-hoc analysis choices has a Type I error rate that may be much higher 鈥?inflated by the implicit multiple comparisons involved in choosing the most significant fork.

**Registered reports** : A more ambitious reform. Journals commit to publish the paper based on the quality of the design and the importance of the question 鈥?_before data collection_. Publication is no longer contingent on statistical significance. This eliminates publication bias at its source: if journals accept null results that arise from well-designed, pre-registered studies, the scientific literature reflects what actually happened rather than what researchers hoped to find.

### 23.6 Adaptive Designs: Efficiency with Statistical Complications

Classical experimental designs are **fixed** : sample size, randomization scheme, and analysis plan are set before any data is collected. But sometimes it is inefficient or unethical to maintain a fixed design when interim data provides relevant information.

**Adaptive designs** allow pre-specified modifications to the design based on interim results:

* **Sequential analysis** : analyze data at multiple interim time points, stopping early if the result is clear (either strong evidence of effect or of futility)
* **Adaptive randomization** : use interim data to shift more participants toward the arm that appears better
* **Sample size re-estimation** : revise the final sample size based on observed variability in interim data

The statistical complication: any flexibility in stopping, allocation, or sample size inflates the Type I error rate if not properly controlled. If you "peek" at data at 50% enrollment and again at 100%, the probability of seeing at least one significant result (even under the null) exceeds 伪\alpha伪.

#### The O'Brien-Fleming Boundary

For sequential testing with pre-specified interim analyses, the **O'Brien-Fleming boundary** is the standard approach. It controls overall Type I error at 伪\alpha伪 by requiring more stringent evidence at early interim analyses (when fewer events have been observed) and relaxing toward 伪\alpha伪 at the final analysis.

For KKK equally spaced interim analyses, the critical value at interim kkk is approximately:

z鈭?z1鈭捨?2鈰匥/kz^* = z_{1-\alpha/2} \cdot \sqrt{K/k}z鈭?z1鈭捨?2鈥嬧媴K/k鈥?
At the first interim (k=1k=1k=1 of K=3K=3K=3 planned): z鈭?1.96脳3鈮?.39z^* = 1.96 \times \sqrt{3} \approx 3.39z鈭?1.96脳3鈥嬧増3.39. At the final analysis (k=3k=3k=3 of K=3K=3K=3): z鈭?1.96脳1=1.96z^* = 1.96 \times \sqrt{1} = 1.96z鈭?1.96脳1鈥?1.96.

Early stopping requires overwhelming evidence; the final analysis uses the standard threshold. This is the tradeoff: the ability to stop early (saving resources and sparing participants from inferior treatment) costs some statistical efficiency.

**Ethical note** : Adaptive designs raise the question of stopping rules and data monitoring committees. Clinical trials typically have independent data monitoring committees (DMCs) 鈥?statisticians and clinicians who see unblinded interim data and recommend stopping or modification, while the research team remains blinded. This separation of roles is essential for maintaining the integrity of the pre-specified analysis.

### 23.7 Thread B Conclusion: The Full Reform Agenda

We have now seen the complete set of reforms that the replication crisis demanded:

Problem (Chapters 9-10) | Cause | Reform (Chapters 9-13, 23)  
---|---|---  
p-hacking | Garden of forking paths | **Pre-registration**  
Underpowered studies | Sample sizes not designed for effect | **Power analysis before data collection**  
Publication bias | Only significant results published | **Registered reports** ; null result journals  
Multiple comparisons | Testing many outcomes, reporting fewest | **Pre-specify primary outcome** ; FWER/FDR correction  
HARKing | Presenting post-hoc hypotheses as a priori | **Pre-registration distinguishes confirmatory from exploratory**  
Confounding | Unmeasured third variables | **Randomization** ; pre-specification of covariates  
Replication failure | Poor designs not requiring replication | **Open data, materials, code** ; direct replication  
  
Each reform addresses a specific vulnerability. Pre-registration addresses the flexibility in analysis choices. Power analysis addresses the epidemic of underpowered studies that produce noisy, non-replicable estimates. Registered reports address publication bias. Randomization, blocking, and factorial designs address the data quality problem at the source.

The reforms are mutually reinforcing. A pre-registered, adequately powered, randomized study with an open data policy is not just better along one dimension 鈥?it is harder to game, easier to replicate, and more trustworthy for all the reasons combined.

This does not mean that every study can follow every reform. Ethical constraints prevent randomization in many medical contexts; resource constraints limit sample sizes; practical constraints limit randomization in field studies. The reforms represent ideals to approximate, not requirements that make imperfect studies worthless. Observational studies with honest acknowledgment of limitations and well-designed causal inference methods (Chapter 18) remain enormously valuable. The goal is to be honest about what each design can and cannot establish.

### 23.8 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** A pharmaceutical company is testing a new antidepressant. They design the trial as follows: patients who choose to enroll receive the drug; patients who are reluctant to take medication receive the placebo. Identify all the problems with this design.

**Answer:**

This design has three fundamental flaws:

**Flaw 1 鈥?No randomization, complete confounding** : Patients are not randomly assigned to drug or placebo. Instead, treatment is determined by patient preference (willingness to take medication). People who are willing to take medication may differ systematically from those who are reluctant in ways that affect depression outcomes: they may be more motivated to engage in treatment, more compliant with follow-up appointments, more likely to make lifestyle changes alongside medication, or have different beliefs about their condition (placebo response is larger in patients who believe they are being treated).

Any observed difference in outcomes between the drug and placebo group reflects a combination of (a) the drug's true effect and (b) these systematic differences between groups. The two are completely confounded.

**Flaw 2 鈥?No blinding** : Patients know whether they received the drug or placebo. This enables placebo effects (patients who believe they are being treated often improve), social desirability bias (patients on the drug may report more improvement to please the researchers), and measurement bias. In depression trials, subjective improvement ratings are a primary outcome 鈥?exactly the kind of outcome most susceptible to expectation effects.

**Flaw 3 鈥?Likely no power analysis** : The design as described says nothing about sample size determination. If the sample size is chosen by convenience or budget rather than power analysis, the study may be dramatically underpowered, incapable of detecting a real effect even if one exists.

**Correct design** : Double-blind randomized controlled trial with allocation concealment (neither patient nor clinician knows assignment until analysis), pre-specified primary outcome (e.g., HDRS score at 8 weeks), pre-registration, and sample size from power analysis based on the minimum clinically meaningful improvement.

* * *

**Q2.** What is blocking? Why does it improve statistical power compared to complete randomization?

**Answer:** Blocking is dividing experimental units into groups (blocks) of similar units _before randomization_ , then randomizing treatment assignment within each block separately.

**Why blocking improves power** :

Statistical power depends on the ability to detect the treatment signal above the background noise. In a completely randomized design, variability between experimental units contributes to the error variance 鈥?it is part of the "noise." If fields in a farming experiment vary greatly in baseline fertility, this variability makes it harder to see the effect of fertilizer.

Blocking converts between-block variability from noise into a systematic, estimable effect. In the analysis, we compare treatment vs. control _within each block_ , effectively subtracting out the block effect. Only the within-block variability (much smaller than total variability) remains as noise. The standard error of the estimated treatment effect is smaller 鈥?meaning shorter confidence intervals and higher power for the same sample size.

Formal statement: the variance of the estimated treatment effect in a randomized block design is approximately:

Var(蟿^)鈭澫僿ithin2=蟽total2鈭捪僢etween blocks2\text{Var}(\hat{\tau}) \propto \sigma^2_{\text{within}} = \sigma^2_{\text{total}} - \sigma^2_{\text{between blocks}}Var(蟿^)鈭澫僿ithin2鈥?蟽total2鈥嬧垝蟽between blocks2鈥?
By making blocks homogeneous, we maximize 蟽between blocks2\sigma^2_{\text{between blocks}}蟽between blocks2鈥?(absorbing variability into blocks), minimizing 蟽within2\sigma^2_{\text{within}}蟽within2鈥?(what remains as error).

**In practice** : Blocking is most valuable when the blocking variable is strongly related to the outcome. If blocks are no more homogeneous than randomly formed groups, blocking costs degrees of freedom without reducing error variance 鈥?a net loss. Block on variables you know (or strongly suspect) are important sources of variability.

* * *

**Q3.** Explain pre-registration. Why does it fix the p-hacking problem? What can a researcher legitimately do after data collection that was not pre-registered?

**Answer:**

**Pre-registration** is the act of publicly committing 鈥?with a time-stamped, publicly accessible document 鈥?to the study's hypothesis, design, primary outcome measure, sample size, and analysis plan _before any data is collected_.

**Why it fixes p-hacking** : p-hacking exploits the undisclosed flexibility in the garden of forking paths 鈥?the researcher can choose, post-hoc, which outcome to report, which covariates to include, which participants to exclude, and which test to use, selecting the combination that achieves significance. This flexibility means the reported p-value reflects not just the probability of the data under the null hypothesis of the stated analysis, but the probability of _any analysis_ of this data producing a significant result.

Pre-registration eliminates this flexibility retrospectively. If the primary analysis was pre-specified, observers can verify that the reported analysis is the one that was planned 鈥?not selected from among many. A pre-registered p-value of 0.04 has a genuine Type I error rate of 0.05 (for that single, pre-specified test). An unregistered p-value of 0.04 from an unspecified analysis may have a much higher true Type I error rate.

**What remains legitimate post-registration** :

Everything is permitted 鈥?but it must be clearly labeled. Researchers may:

* Run any exploratory analyses they wish after data collection
* Re-examine the data through different statistical lenses
* Test hypotheses that occurred to them after seeing the data
* Investigate unexpected patterns

The requirement is transparency: these analyses must be clearly labeled as **exploratory** or **post-hoc** , not **confirmatory**. Exploratory findings are hypotheses to be tested in future pre-registered studies, not conclusions from the current study. The distinction is not between "allowed" and "not allowed" 鈥?it is between "this was predicted and is confirmatory" and "this was suggested by the data and needs replication."

**Q4.** Explain factorial designs. A company wants to test three variables: (1) email subject line (A vs. B), (2) discount amount (10% vs. 20%), and (3) time of day of send (morning vs. evening). How many conditions does a full factorial design require? How many conditions would a one-factor-at-a-time approach require to answer the same three questions? Why is the factorial approach more efficient, and what additional information does it provide?

**Answer:**

**Full factorial design conditions** : A 2脳2脳22 \times 2 \times 22脳2脳2 factorial design (3 binary factors) requires 23=82^3 = 823=8 conditions: all combinations of (A/B) 脳 (10%/20%) 脳 (morning/evening):

Subject | Discount | Time | Condition  
---|---|---|---  
A | 10% | Morning | 1  
A | 10% | Evening | 2  
A | 20% | Morning | 3  
A | 20% | Evening | 4  
B | 10% | Morning | 5  
B | 10% | Evening | 6  
B | 20% | Morning | 7  
B | 20% | Evening | 8  
  
**One-factor-at-a-time (OFAT) approach** : To test 3 questions, OFAT runs 3 separate two-arm experiments, each varying one factor while holding the others fixed. With a baseline condition and 3 factors each requiring a comparison, OFAT needs 4 conditions total (1 baseline + 3 "changed" conditions). However, OFAT requires more observations overall because the baseline condition's sample is not shared across all comparisons 鈥?each experiment needs its own control arm. Effectively, OFAT requires 3脳2=63 \times 2 = 63脳2=6 condition-assignments to answer 3 questions, versus 8 for the factorial. For the same statistical power, OFAT uses more total observations: factorial efficiency gain comes from each factor being estimated using all observations, not just half.

**Why factorial is more efficient** : In the full factorial, the main effect of subject line (A vs. B) is estimated by comparing all 4 conditions with A (conditions 1,2,3,4) against all 4 conditions with B (conditions 5,6,7,8). All 8 conditions' data contributes to every main effect estimate. In OFAT, only the 2 conditions in the subject line experiment contribute to the subject line estimate. The factorial design uses the same observations to estimate 3 main effects simultaneously 鈥?this "hidden replication" is the efficiency source.

**Additional information 鈥?interactions** : The factorial design allows estimating all **interaction effects** that OFAT cannot detect:

* Does the subject line effect depend on the discount amount? (A脳B interaction)
* Does the subject line effect depend on time of day? (A脳C interaction)
* Does the discount effect depend on time of day? (B脳C interaction)
* Three-way interaction: Does the combination of all three factors matter?

OFAT, by design, holds other factors constant and thus cannot detect interactions. If Subject line B works better than A only when paired with a 20% discount (an interaction), OFAT will report an average effect across discount levels 鈥?potentially missing that the combination matters. Factorial designs reveal not just what works, but when and under what conditions.

**Q2.** A tech company runs an A/B test for a new product recommendation algorithm. They run the test for 2 weeks and find p = 0.07 for the primary metric (7-day retention). Their product manager says "just run it for another week until we hit significance."

(a) Explain the statistical problem with this approach. (b) What is the correct way to handle this situation? (c) If the company wanted the flexibility to look at results weekly and stop early, what statistical approach should they have pre-specified?

**Answer:**

**(a) The statistical problem 鈥?optional stopping** :

"Running longer until significant" is optional stopping 鈥?the experiment continues or terminates based on the current p-value. This inflates the Type I error rate far above the nominal 伪\alpha伪.

Consider the following: at each analysis, there is a chance of observing p 鈮?0.05 by chance. If you analyze after 2 weeks, then after 3 weeks, then after 4 weeks 鈥?that is three chances to observe a false positive. The probability of at least one false positive across three independent tests at 伪=0.05\alpha = 0.05伪=0.05 is approximately 1鈭?1鈭?.05)3=0.1431 - (1-0.05)^3 = 0.1431鈭?1鈭?.05)3=0.143, not 0.05. By continuing to test until significance is reached, the true Type I error rate can be substantially higher than 0.05.

More practically: the p = 0.07 result at 2 weeks suggests the effect (if real) is small or the sample is underpowered. Running longer and continuing to re-examine is exactly the p-hacking procedure discussed in Chapter 9 鈥?a garden-of-forking-paths where the stopping decision is made based on the data.

**(b) Correct approach** :

The experiment should have had a pre-specified duration 鈥?based on a power analysis 鈥?before any data was collected. If the pre-specified duration was 2 weeks and p = 0.07 was observed, the correct conclusion is:

* Either the effect is real but the study was underpowered (too small to detect it at 伪=0.05\alpha = 0.05伪=0.05)
* Or the effect does not exist and p = 0.07 is consistent with the null

In either case, the result is p = 0.07 from a pre-specified 2-week test. The company should report this as "marginal, non-significant evidence (p = 0.07)." If the effect size is of practical interest (the point estimate is worth having), plan a new pre-registered study powered to detect the observed effect size.

Extending the existing experiment invalidates the Type I error guarantee. Starting a new pre-registered experiment is the statistically honest approach.

**(c) Pre-specified sequential analysis** :

If the company wanted to check results weekly, they should have pre-specified a sequential analysis plan using an error-spending approach such as **O'Brien-Fleming boundaries**. This plan:

  1. **Pre-specifies** the number and timing of interim analyses (e.g., weeks 1, 2, 3, 4)
  2. **Adjusts the critical value** at each analysis to control overall Type I error at 0.05
  3. **Sets the early stopping criterion** at a stringent threshold for early weeks and relaxes it toward 0.05 at the final analysis

For example, with 4 weekly analyses, the critical value at week 1 might be z鈭?3.92z^* = 3.92z鈭?3.92 (very stringent), declining to z鈭?1.96z^* = 1.96z鈭?1.96 at week 4. The experiment stops early only if the evidence is overwhelming early on 鈥?otherwise, it continues to the pre-specified end.

This gives the company the flexibility to stop early if the effect is unmistakably large, while maintaining the statistical integrity of the final analysis if no early stopping occurs.

#### Think Deeper

**Q2.** Randomization is considered the gold standard for causal inference, but some argue it creates its own problems: randomized trials enroll selected volunteers, which may not represent the population the treatment will be applied to; rare harms may not appear in trials of any feasible size; and randomization is often infeasible or unethical.

Describe three scenarios where randomization is not the best available option and explain what alternative design would provide the strongest available evidence in each case.

**Discussion:**

**Scenario 1 鈥?Ethical impossibility: Does smoking cause lung cancer?**

We cannot randomize humans to smoke for decades. The best available evidence came from a combination of: (a) large prospective cohort studies with careful exposure measurement, (b) a dose-response relationship (more smoking 鈫?more cancer), (c) consistency across studies in many countries and populations, (d) a plausible biological mechanism (carcinogens in tobacco), and (e) animal experiments that provided experimental evidence of a mechanism.

The Bradford Hill criteria formalize how to make causal claims without randomization: strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experimental analogy, and analogy. No single study substitutes for randomization, but a preponderance of evidence across multiple lines of evidence 鈥?each ruling out different alternative explanations 鈥?can achieve high confidence in causal conclusions.

**Scenario 2 鈥?Infeasible scale: Does access to a minimum wage increase reduce poverty?**

We cannot randomize states or countries to minimum wage laws. The best available design is a **difference-in-differences (DiD)** analysis exploiting natural policy variation: states that raised their minimum wage serve as "treated" units; neighboring states without increases serve as "controls." Card and Krueger's famous study of New Jersey vs. Pennsylvania is the canonical example.

DiD is strongest when: (a) pre-treatment trends in treated and control groups are parallel (validating the counterfactual assumption), (b) there is no other policy change that affected treated but not control states at the same time (no confounding policy changes), and (c) the treatment assignment has plausible exogeneity (the policy change was not caused by labor market conditions that would have produced the outcome anyway). The limitations are explicit: the parallel trends assumption is untestable but can be partially validated.

**Scenario 3 鈥?Rare events: Does a rare drug side effect (1 in 10,000 patients) cause long-term kidney damage?**

A randomized trial adequate to detect a 1/10,000 rate would require millions of participants 鈥?infeasible. The best available evidence comes from: (a) **pharmacovigilance databases** (large observational registries of drug exposure and outcomes), (b) **case-control studies** (comparing patients with kidney damage to matched controls on drug exposure), and (c) **self-controlled case series** (comparing each patient's rate of kidney damage during drug exposure vs. non-exposure periods, eliminating between-person confounding).

The self-controlled design is particularly powerful for rare events because each patient serves as their own control 鈥?eliminating all time-invariant confounders. It requires only that the outcome is independent of exposure timing (no confounding by indication that changes over the exposure period).

In all three scenarios, the goal is the same as randomization: eliminate or account for confounding to isolate the causal effect. The tools differ because the constraints differ. Statistical thinking requires knowing when the gold standard is unavailable and which next-best design provides the most credible evidence under the circumstances.

* * *

**Q1.** Pre-registration has been criticized on the grounds that it stifles scientific creativity 鈥?that some of the most important discoveries in science were unexpected findings from exploratory data analysis rather than confirmed hypotheses. Evaluate this criticism. How should we distinguish between confirmatory and exploratory research, and what role should each play in the scientific enterprise?

**Discussion:**

The criticism has genuine merit. Many important scientific discoveries 鈥?the structure of DNA, the role of H. pylori in ulcers, the acceleration of the universe's expansion 鈥?involved unexpected observations that did not fit the hypothesis being tested. A rigid requirement that all science be pre-registered would eliminate the exploratory research that generates the hypotheses worth confirming.

But the criticism misunderstands what pre-registration advocates actually argue.

**What pre-registration is for** : Pre-registration is designed for _confirmatory_ research 鈥?studies that test a specific, pre-formed hypothesis with a primary outcome measure. The goal is to ensure that "this study confirmed the hypothesis" means something statistically. When you pre-register a hypothesis and then observe p < 0.05, you have genuine evidence (at the claimed Type I error rate) for the hypothesis.

**What exploratory research should look like** : Exploratory research 鈥?"what patterns exist in this data?" 鈥?is legitimate, valuable, and does not require pre-registration. But exploratory findings must be labeled as such. An exploratory finding is a hypothesis. A confirmed hypothesis has been tested in an independent pre-registered study. The error in the pre-registration debate is treating exploratory findings as if they were confirmatory.

**The pragmatic resolution** : Science needs both. The scientific process should look like:

  1. Exploratory phase: analyze data freely, generate hypotheses, identify unexpected patterns, publish as "exploratory" or "hypothesis-generating"
  2. Confirmatory phase: pre-register the most promising hypotheses, collect new data, test them with appropriate Type I error control

The replication crisis arose because step 2 was missing 鈥?exploratory findings were published as if they were confirmatory, without the verification step. Pre-registration does not prevent serendipity; it ensures that serendipitous findings are honestly labeled and eventually verified.

### Chapter Summary

Good experimental design prevents errors that no statistical analysis can fix after the fact. The three pillars 鈥?**randomization** (distribution of confounders by chance), **replication** (multiple units per treatment for error estimation), and **control** (a meaningful comparison baseline) 鈥?are the foundation of experiments that can answer causal questions.

**Blocking** reduces the impact of known sources of variability by grouping similar units before randomization. It converts variability into a systematic component that is estimated and subtracted, leaving a cleaner residual error and greater statistical power.

**Power analysis** determines sample size before data collection, based on the minimum effect size of practical importance, the desired power, and the Type I error rate. Underpowered studies contribute to the replication crisis by generating noisy, non-reproducible estimates. Overpowered studies waste resources and may be unethical.

**Factorial designs** test multiple factors simultaneously, estimating main effects and interactions with greater efficiency than separate single-factor experiments.

**Pre-registration** 鈥?publicly committing to the analysis plan before data collection 鈥?is the institutional fix for the garden-of-forking-paths problem. It does not constrain exploratory analysis; it requires honest labeling of what is confirmatory vs. exploratory.

**Adaptive designs** (sequential analysis, adaptive randomization) provide flexibility to stop early or modify the design based on interim data, but require careful statistical planning (error-spending boundaries, DMCs) to maintain Type I error control.

Thread B reaches its conclusion: the replication crisis was not merely a problem of researchers behaving badly 鈥?it was a problem of institutional structures that did not demand good design. Pre-registration, power analysis, registered reports, and open data are the structural reforms that make the scientific process robust to the human tendency to find what we are looking for.

In the next chapter, we turn to a specific but pervasive design challenge: surveying populations when we can only observe a sample.
