## Chapter 24: Survey Methodology and Sampling

In 1936, the Literary Digest mailed ten million ballots to Americans, asking who they would vote for in the upcoming presidential election. Over two million people responded 鈥?an enormous sample by any measure. The magazine confidently predicted that Alf Landon would defeat Franklin D. Roosevelt in a landslide. Roosevelt won 61% of the popular vote and 46 of 48 states.

The Literary Digest was finished. It folded the following year.

What went wrong? Not the math. With 2.3 million respondents, the margin of error from sampling variability was negligible. The problem was not how many people were surveyed; it was _who_ was surveyed. The Literary Digest mailed to automobile owners, telephone subscribers, and its own readers. In 1936 鈥?still in the depths of the Great Depression 鈥?owning a car or a telephone was a marker of wealth. The survey had systematically excluded poor and working-class voters, who overwhelmingly supported Roosevelt.

This is the foundational lesson of survey methodology: **a large biased sample is worse than a small representative one.** The Literary Digest had two million observations of the wrong question: not "how will Americans vote?" but "how will wealthy Americans who respond to mail ballots vote?"

In the same election, a young pollster named George Gallup predicted a Roosevelt landslide based on just 3,000 carefully chosen respondents. He was right because he sampled representatively, not because he sampled more. The entire machinery of modern survey research grew from this lesson.

### 24.1 What Makes a Sample Representative?

A sample is **representative** if it has the same distribution of relevant characteristics as the population from which it is drawn. A survey of voter preferences that has the same age distribution, income distribution, geographic distribution, and political history as the voting population will 鈥?under good statistical conditions 鈥?give accurate estimates of voting preferences.

But "representative" is harder to achieve than it sounds, because we usually do not know the full joint distribution of all relevant characteristics in the population. We can try to match a sample on age, income, and education 鈥?but a sample that matches on these three variables may still be unrepresentative on political attitudes, media consumption habits, or social networks in ways that affect voting.

#### The Sampling Frame

Before drawing any sample, we need a **sampling frame** : a list (or operational equivalent) of all units in the target population. The sampling frame defines who could potentially be sampled.

Sampling frames are never perfect. A telephone directory includes only people with listed phone numbers. A patient registry includes only patients who have sought medical care at that institution. A social media user list includes only people with accounts. Each frame excludes some portion of the population 鈥?and excluded groups may differ systematically from included groups in ways that bias estimates.

The Literary Digest's frame (automobile owners, telephone subscribers, subscribers) was the fundamental error: the frame excluded the population most likely to vote differently from the frame population.

Good survey design begins with asking: who is excluded from my sampling frame, and how might they differ from the included population?

### 24.2 Probability vs. Non-Probability Sampling

All rigorous survey methodology is built on **probability sampling** : every unit in the population has a known, non-zero probability of being selected. This allows:

  1. Unbiased estimation: the sample statistics will, on average, equal the population parameters
  2. Valid uncertainty quantification: sampling error can be computed from the design

**Non-probability sampling** (convenience samples, self-selected respondents, snowball samples) violates both. The Literary Digest survey was non-probability: wealthy people who responded to mail ballots chose whether to participate. We cannot compute a valid standard error for a convenience sample because we do not know who was excluded or why.

#### Common Probability Sampling Designs

**Simple random sampling (SRS)** : Draw nnn units from a population of NNN at random (each unit has probability n/Nn/Nn/N of selection). Simple and unbiased, but often inefficient or impractical for large populations.

**Stratified random sampling** : Divide the population into non-overlapping strata (subgroups) and draw a random sample from each stratum separately.

渭^strat=鈭慼=1HWhy藟h\hat{\mu}_{\text{strat}} = \sum_{h=1}^{H} W_h \bar{y}_h渭^鈥媠trat鈥?h=1鈭慔鈥媁h鈥媦藟鈥媓鈥?
where Wh=Nh/NW_h = N_h/NWh鈥?Nh鈥?N is the stratum population weight and y藟h\bar{y}_hy藟鈥媓鈥?is the sample mean in stratum hhh.

Advantages: (a) guarantees representation of all strata; (b) if strata are homogeneous within but different between, stratified sampling is more efficient than SRS 鈥?the within-stratum variance is smaller than the total variance. This is the survey analogy of blocking in experiments.

**Cluster sampling** : Divide the population into clusters (e.g., schools, census tracts, hospitals), randomly select clusters, and survey everyone (or a random sub-sample) within selected clusters.

Used when a complete sampling frame for individuals is unavailable or when it would be too expensive to send interviewers to all geographic locations. The trade-off: individuals within a cluster are more similar to each other than to individuals in other clusters (intracluster correlation, ICC). This reduces the effective sample size below the nominal sample size.

The **design effect (DEFF)** accounts for this:

DEFF=1+(m鈭?)鈰匢CC\text{DEFF} = 1 + (m-1) \cdot \text{ICC}DEFF=1+(m鈭?)鈰匢CC

where mmm is the average cluster size and ICC is the intracluster correlation. An effective sample size of n/DEFFn/\text{DEFF}n/DEFF 鈥?not nnn 鈥?should be used in variance computations. Ignoring clustering in analysis is a very common error that produces confidence intervals that are too narrow and p-values that are too small.

**Systematic sampling** : Sample every kkkth unit from a list (e.g., every 10th patient on a waiting list). Efficient and easy to implement. Assumes the list order is not periodic in a way that aligns with the sampling interval.

### 24.3 Sources of Bias in Surveys

Even with probability sampling, surveys face several sources of bias that are not captured in the simple sampling error formula.

#### Non-Response Bias

**Non-response bias** is the most pervasive modern survey problem. It arises when the people who respond to a survey differ systematically from those who do not.

Response rates for telephone polls have fallen from approximately 80% in the 1990s to below 10% today. If 90% of people hang up, the 10% who respond are not a random subset of the population 鈥?they are, at minimum, people willing to answer surveys. Whether they differ in politically or substantively relevant ways depends on the survey topic.

The crucial question is not "what fraction responded?" but "do non-responders differ from responders on the outcome of interest?" If Democrats are more likely than Republicans to respond to political surveys (differential non-response), a random sample of the sampling frame 鈥?properly drawn 鈥?will over-represent Democratic opinion. This cannot be fixed by increasing sample size; it is a systematic bias.

#### Measurement Bias

**Measurement bias** (or response bias) occurs when the survey responses themselves are systematically inaccurate:

* **Social desirability bias** : respondents report behaviors or attitudes they think are expected or approved rather than their true views. Surveys of sensitive topics (drug use, sexual behavior, income) are especially susceptible.
* **Question wording** : "Do you support additional government spending on social programs?" and "Do you support government waste on bloated social programs?" may both refer to the same policy but elicit very different response distributions.
* **Question order** : earlier questions prime respondents to think in certain frames that affect responses to later questions.
* **Mode effects** : telephone, online, and in-person interviews produce different response patterns for the same questions.

#### Coverage Bias

**Coverage bias** (or frame bias) is the Literary Digest problem: the sampling frame systematically excludes a subgroup of the target population. In modern surveys:

* Cell-phone-only households (often younger, more mobile) were excluded when surveys used only landline frames
* Non-internet households are excluded from online surveys
* Non-English speakers are excluded from English-only surveys

### 24.4 Weighting: The Partial Fix

When the achieved sample does not match the target population on known characteristics, **weighting** partially corrects the bias.

**Post-stratification weighting** : after data collection, reweight each respondent so the sample's distribution on known variables (age, gender, education, race, geography) matches the population's distribution from census data.

If young adults (18鈥?9) are 20% of the population but only 10% of survey respondents, we give each young adult respondent a weight of 20/10=220/10 = 220/10=2. Older respondents who are over-represented are down-weighted. Weighted estimates:

渭^weighted=鈭慽wiyi鈭慽wi\hat{\mu}_{\text{weighted}} = \frac{\sum_i w_i y_i}{\sum_i w_i}渭^鈥媤eighted鈥?鈭慽鈥媤i鈥嬧垜i鈥媤i鈥媦i鈥嬧€?
**Why weighting is a partial fix, not a complete one** :

Weighting corrects for known imbalances on measured variables. It cannot correct for imbalances on unmeasured variables. If young Republicans are more willing to respond to political surveys than young Democrats (within the age group), post-stratification on age will not fix this bias 鈥?we have weighted young respondents up, but they are still not representative of young people.

Modern polling uses sophisticated **multilevel regression and post-stratification (MrP)** 鈥?a Bayesian approach that models the response pattern across many demographic cells simultaneously and then aggregates, using the census to set cell weights. MrP is more statistically efficient than simple post-stratification, especially for small subgroups, because it borrows strength across demographic cells.

#### Thread A: Selection Bias in Clinical Trial Enrollment

Selection bias affects not only opinion surveys but clinical research. A clinical trial is only valuable to the extent that its findings generalize to patients in clinical practice. But who enrolls in trials?

Clinical trials typically exclude patients who:

* Have multiple serious comorbidities (complicates attribution of outcomes to the drug)
* Cannot consent or comply with complex protocols
* Are taking medications that might interact with the trial drug
* Live too far from a trial center to attend follow-up visits

The trial sample 鈥?highly selected, monitored, protocol-compliant 鈥?may differ substantially from the general patient population in ways that affect the treatment's effect. A drug that reduces blood pressure by 5 mmHg in a carefully monitored trial population may reduce it by only 2 mmHg when prescribed in routine clinical practice to patients with multiple comorbidities who miss half their appointments.

This gap between **efficacy** (effect under ideal trial conditions) and **effectiveness** (effect under real-world conditions) is a direct consequence of non-representative sampling. Pragmatic trials 鈥?which use broad eligibility criteria, routine care delivery, and flexible protocols 鈥?address this by sampling from the clinical population of interest rather than an idealized subset.

### 24.5 Margin of Error and What It Does (and Does Not) Tell You

When a poll reports that Candidate A leads with 52%, margin of error 卤3 percentage points, the margin of error refers specifically to the **sampling error** 鈥?the variability due to random sampling from a well-defined population.

For a simple random sample of size nnn estimating a proportion ppp:

Margin of error=z0.975鈰卲(1鈭抪)n\text{Margin of error} = z_{0.975} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}Margin of error=z0.975鈥嬧媴np(1鈭抪)鈥嬧€?
For p=0.5p = 0.5p=0.5 (worst case 鈥?maximizes variance) and n=1,000n = 1,000n=1,000:

MOE=1.96脳0.5脳0.51000=1.96脳0.0158=0.031鈮?.1%\text{MOE} = 1.96 \times \sqrt{\frac{0.5 \times 0.5}{1000}} = 1.96 \times 0.0158 = 0.031 \approx 3.1\%MOE=1.96脳10000.5脳0.5鈥嬧€?1.96脳0.0158=0.031鈮?.1%

So a sample of about 1,000 gives 卤3% margin of error regardless of population size (whether the population is 100,000 or 300 million). This surprises many people 鈥?the absolute size of the sample matters, not its fraction of the population. This follows from the sampling distribution of the sample proportion: p^鈭糔(p,p(1鈭抪)/n)\hat{p} \sim \mathcal{N}(p, p(1-p)/n)p^鈥嬧埣N(p,p(1鈭抪)/n). Population size does not appear.

**What the margin of error does NOT cover** :

* Non-response bias (the Literary Digest problem)
* Measurement bias (question wording, social desirability)
* Coverage bias (excluded subgroups)
* Model error in weighting assumptions
* True uncertainty in reported confidence intervals if the sampling was not truly random

A poll with 卤3% sampling error that has 10% response rate and unknown non-response bias could have a true total error far larger than 卤3%. The margin of error is only the sampling error portion of total survey error 鈥?and in modern polling, sampling error may be the smallest contributor to total error.

### 24.6 Why Election Polls Sometimes Fail

The 2016 US presidential election is the canonical modern example of polling failure. Most polls predicted a comfortable Clinton victory; Trump won the Electoral College. A careful analysis of what went wrong illustrates all the concepts in this chapter.

**Sources of the 2016 polling failure** :

  1. **Non-response bias 鈥?differential by education** : College-educated voters respond to surveys at higher rates than non-college voters. In 2016, Trump outperformed Clinton dramatically among non-college whites 鈥?a group that was systematically under-represented even after demographic weighting. Education was not used consistently as a weighting variable.

  2. **Late-deciding voters** : A disproportionate number of voters who made their decision in the final week (some after the Comey letter announcing the re-opening of the Clinton email investigation) broke for Trump. Polls taken earlier did not capture this movement.

  3. **State-level polling failure** : National popular vote estimates were approximately correct (Clinton won the popular vote). But Electoral College outcomes depend on state-level results. Some key states (Michigan, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania) were under-polled, and where polled, the non-response bias patterns were acute.

  4. **Herding** : Polling organizations are reluctant to publish results dramatically different from other polls. This creates correlation between published polls 鈥?if one poll has a systematic bias, others may suppress findings that differ. Aggregating correlated polls does not reduce error as fast as aggregating independent polls.

The 2020 election had even larger polling errors in some states (Trump over-performance was larger than in 2016) despite post-2016 efforts to correct for education weighting. This suggests non-response bias has continued to worsen 鈥?in ways that post-stratification on measured demographics cannot fully correct 鈥?because the respondents willing to answer polls may differ from non-respondents in their political attitudes in ways not captured by education, age, race, or geography alone.

### 24.7 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Explain the difference between sampling error and non-response bias. Why can increasing sample size fix sampling error but not non-response bias?

**Answer:**

**Sampling error** arises from the randomness of which units are selected from the population. Even with perfect probability sampling and 100% response, there is random variation in sample statistics from sample to sample. This error:

* Decreases as sample size nnn increases (proportional to 1/n1/\sqrt{n}1/n鈥?
* Can be computed and quantified as the margin of error
* Is fully captured by the confidence interval formula for probability samples

**Non-response bias** arises when sampled units that respond differ systematically from those that do not respond. If a survey of political preferences has 30% response rate, and Democrats are more likely to respond than Republicans (among those sampled), the survey will overestimate Democratic support even if the sampling was perfectly random.

**Why increasing sample size cannot fix non-response bias** :

Increasing sample size increases the number of respondents but not the fraction of the target population that responds. If 70% of people contacted hang up, doubling the sample contact list produces twice as many respondents 鈥?but those respondents are drawn from the same 30% who were willing to respond. The respondents still systematically differ from non-respondents in the same way. The bias is not reduced; only the sampling error around the biased estimate is reduced.

This is a crucial distinction: the margin of error tells you about precision (sampling error), not about accuracy (bias). A biased estimate can have very small sampling error 鈥?it consistently gives the wrong answer.

* * *

**Q2.** A survey of 1,200 adults estimates that 54% support a new policy, with a margin of error of 卤2.8% at the 95% confidence level. A journalist writes: "The poll shows that a majority of Americans support the policy." Evaluate this conclusion.

**Answer:**

The journalist's conclusion is overstated in several ways:

**Issue 1 鈥?The sample is not "Americans"** : "Americans" implies the general US adult population. The margin of error tells us about sampling variability only 鈥?not about how representative the sample is. If the survey was conducted online and only adults with internet access and willingness to participate in online surveys were included (convenience or panel sample), the finding does not generalize to all Americans.

**Issue 2 鈥?54% 卤 2.8% spans below 50%** : The 95% confidence interval is approximately 51.2% to 56.8%. The lower bound is above 50%, so there is statistical evidence that support exceeds 50% 鈥?but barely. With margin of error 卤2.8%, the result is not far above the threshold for "majority." Calling it a "majority" is technically supported at 95% confidence, but describing it as a stable majority is premature.

**Issue 3 鈥?Total survey error vs. sampling error** : The 卤2.8% margin of error covers only sampling error (the randomness of sample selection). It does not cover non-response bias, question wording effects, or coverage bias. If the question was worded favorably toward the policy, or if policy supporters responded at higher rates, the true population support could be below 50% even if the reported estimate is 54%.

**More accurate statement** : "A survey of 1,200 adults found 54% support for the policy, with a sampling margin of error of 卤2.8% (95% CI). Subject to the usual caveats about survey response rates and question wording, this suggests support may exceed 50%, though total uncertainty is larger than the sampling margin of error alone."

* * *

**Q3.** What is post-stratification weighting? When does it work well, and when is it insufficient?

**Answer:**

**Post-stratification weighting** is a correction technique applied after data collection. After observing that the achieved sample does not match the population on known characteristics, each respondent is assigned a weight that adjusts for their group's under- or over-representation.

For example: if 18鈥?9 year olds are 22% of the population but only 12% of survey respondents, each young respondent receives weight 22/12=1.8322/12 = 1.8322/12=1.83. Older groups that are over-represented receive weights below 1. Weighted estimates then reflect the population distribution.

**When it works well** :

* The weighting variables are available from a reliable census or administrative source
* The weighting variables are strongly related to the survey outcome (so matching on them removes most bias)
* Within each demographic cell, respondents are representative of the cell's population (not just demographically representative but attitudinally representative)
* Non-response is primarily explained by the measured weighting variables

**When it is insufficient** :

* Non-response is related to unmeasured variables (e.g., political enthusiasm, distrust of institutions)
* Within-cell non-response bias: even after matching age, education, and race, respondents within each cell may differ from non-respondents in ways relevant to the survey
* High variability in weights: some demographic cells may have very few respondents, requiring extreme up-weighting that increases sampling variance
* Weighting variables are unmeasured or measured with error (the census itself has coverage errors)

The 2020 polling failures illustrate the limits: polls weighted on age, education, race, and geography still systematically over-represented Biden supporters within demographic groups 鈥?because the kind of person who responds to political polls in 2020 was not representative of voters within demographic cells. Post-stratification corrects for compositional differences in observable demographics but cannot correct for unobservable attitudinal differences between respondents and non-respondents.

**Q4.** What is multilevel regression and post-stratification (MrP)? How does it differ from simple post-stratification weighting, and why might it perform better for estimating opinions in small geographic areas?

**Answer:**

**Simple post-stratification** (Chapter 24.4) re-weights respondents so the sample's distribution on measured demographic variables (age, gender, race, education) matches the population's distribution from census data. Each respondent receives a weight inversely proportional to the over- or under-representation of their demographic cell. Simple and transparent, but degrades when some demographic cells have very few respondents 鈥?a cell with 2 respondents will be up-weighted enormously if that cell is 15% of the population, producing highly variable estimates.

**MrP (multilevel regression and post-stratification)** addresses this by: (1) fitting a multilevel statistical model that predicts the survey outcome as a function of individual demographics and geography, using the hierarchical model to borrow strength across geographic units; (2) applying the model to the census joint distribution of all demographic cells to generate population estimates.

Concretely: instead of computing the mean opinion among the 3 respondents in a rural county, MrP estimates the county's opinion from a model that partially pools information from all respondents across all counties, adjusting for each county's demographic composition. A small county's estimate is "shrunk" toward a weighted average of similar counties, reducing the variance from small cell counts.

**Why MrP performs better for small areas** :

Direct estimates from small geographic areas (districts, counties, zip codes) often have very small sample sizes 鈥?sometimes 0鈥? respondents. Post-stratification with small cells produces extremely noisy estimates. MrP's hierarchical model uses a **partial pooling** approach: estimates from small areas borrow strength from larger areas with similar demographics. The resulting estimates are biased toward the pooled mean but have dramatically lower variance 鈥?the bias-variance tradeoff applied to spatial estimation.

The key assumption MrP makes: geographic variation in opinion is partially explained by demographics (compositional effects) plus area-level fixed effects estimated from larger patterns. If this assumption holds, MrP outperforms direct estimates, especially for rare subgroups or small areas. The approach was developed by Gelman and collaborators and has become standard for small-area estimation in political science, epidemiology, and public health.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** A health researcher wants to estimate the prevalence of depression among adults in a large US city. She designs a survey with three sampling options:

**Option A** : Stand outside shopping malls during daytime hours and recruit passersby (n = 500)

**Option B** : Randomly sample 500 names from the city's voter registration rolls, mail paper questionnaires (expected 25% response rate = 125 responses)

**Option C** : Use stratified random sampling of the city's census tracts (stratified by income quartile), then within each stratum, randomly call telephone numbers from a commercial list, with mobile and landline coverage (n = 400)

Evaluate each option's strengths and limitations for estimating depression prevalence.

Hint

Consider: who is excluded from the sampling frame, what the response rate implies, and what characteristics might differ between responders and non-responders.

**Answer:**

**Option A 鈥?Mall intercepts** :

_Strengths_ : Easy, fast, low cost. May achieve a high completion rate among those approached.

_Limitations_ :

* **Severe coverage bias** : Only people who shop at malls during daytime hours are accessible. This excludes people who work full-time during weekday hours (missing a large working population), people who avoid malls (including those with social anxiety 鈥?directly relevant to depression prevalence), homeless individuals, elderly and mobility-impaired individuals, and those from neighborhoods without nearby malls.
* **Not probability sampling** : We have no way of knowing the probability that any given city resident appears at this mall at this time.
* This is a convenience sample. Standard errors and confidence intervals cannot be validly computed. Estimates will not generalize to the city population.

_Verdict_ : Unsuitable for population-level prevalence estimation. Might be useful for a qualitative pilot study.

**Option B 鈥?Voter registration rolls** :

_Strengths_ : Voter registration rolls are a reasonably complete frame for registered voters. Probability sampling (simple random sample) allows valid standard errors.

_Limitations_ :

* **Coverage bias** : Voter registration excludes: non-citizens (approximately 14% of the US population), unregistered eligible voters (about 30% of adults), and people who have moved without updating registration. If unregistered voters have different depression rates (younger people and those with less stable housing are both more likely to be unregistered and more likely to have depression), estimates will be biased.
* **Non-response bias** : Mail surveys with 25% response rates are problematic. The 75% who do not respond may differ from those who do. People with severe depression may be less likely to complete and return a mail questionnaire. This would underestimate depression prevalence.
* **Paper format** : Self-report depression measures may be affected by reading ability and questionnaire burden.

_Verdict_ : Better than Option A (probability sampling from a defined frame), but coverage and non-response bias are significant concerns.

**Option C 鈥?Stratified telephone survey with mobile and landline** :

_Strengths_ :

* **Stratified sampling** ensures representation across income levels (important: depression rates vary substantially by income).
* **Mobile and landline** coverage substantially reduces the coverage bias from cell-phone-only households 鈥?a major problem with landline-only surveys.
* **Probability sampling** with stratification allows valid confidence intervals, and stratification typically improves efficiency.

_Limitations_ :

* **Non-response bias** : Even well-designed telephone surveys have low response rates. People with depression may be less likely to answer unknown calls.
* **Telephone coverage** : Still excludes those with neither cell nor landline (rare but not zero 鈥?approximately 1鈥?% of adults, often very poor).
* **Social desirability** : Some people may underreport depression symptoms by telephone, especially if a household member can overhear.

_Verdict_ : Best of the three options. Probability sampling, reasonable frame coverage, stratification to ensure representation of income groups. Non-response bias remains a concern 鈥?should be addressed by comparing achieved sample demographics to census data and applying post-stratification weights.

**Recommendation** : Option C, supplemented by post-stratification weighting on age, gender, race, and income to adjust for any non-response imbalances identified by comparison with census data.

**Q2.** A national political polling organization wants to estimate support for a ballot measure in each of 50 US states. They have a national random sample of 3,000 respondents.

(a) If respondents are distributed proportionally to state population, how many respondents would the smallest states have (e.g., Wyoming with ~0.17% of the US population)? (b) A simple post-stratification approach computes each state's support as the weighted mean of that state's respondents. What problem arises for small states? (c) The organization adopts MrP. Briefly describe how MrP would handle the Wyoming estimation problem. (d) The poll is trying to predict how each state will vote. What factor does the sampling margin of error not address, and why does this limit the poll's usefulness for Electoral College predictions?

Hint

For (a): 0.0017 脳 3000. For (d): think about what the margin of error captures and what it doesn't.

**Answer:**

**(a) Wyoming sample size** : 0.0017脳3000鈮?0.0017 \times 3000 \approx 50.0017脳3000鈮? respondents. With a 50% response rate in practice, the usable Wyoming sample might be 2鈥? respondents.

**(b) Problem with simple post-stratification for small states** : With 5 respondents from Wyoming, the estimated proportion supporting the ballot measure is essentially the mean of 5 binary responses. The standard error is approximately 0.5脳0.5/5=0.224\sqrt{0.5 \times 0.5 / 5} = 0.2240.5脳0.5/5鈥?0.224 鈥?a 95% CI spanning 44 percentage points. Any estimate will be dominated by sampling noise. Post-stratification adjusting for age, race, and education within Wyoming still works with these 5 respondents, but the resulting estimate is extremely unreliable.

Worse, if some demographic cells in Wyoming have zero respondents, post-stratification cannot fill in those cells 鈥?the weighting procedure cannot upweight respondents who do not exist.

**(c) MrP approach for Wyoming** : MrP would:

  1. Fit a multilevel logistic regression of ballot support on individual demographics (age, gender, education, race) and state-level predictors (partisan lean, income, rurality). The model includes a random effect for each state.

  2. The random effect for Wyoming is estimated with high uncertainty (very few Wyoming respondents), but the hierarchical model partially pools it toward nearby states (Idaho, Montana) and toward states with similar demographics 鈥?borrowing strength.

  3. Apply the fitted model to Wyoming's actual demographic distribution from the census to predict ballot support for each demographic cell in Wyoming, then aggregate.

The result: a Wyoming estimate informed by both Wyoming's few respondents and by information from similar states and similar demographic groups elsewhere in the data. The estimate is biased toward the pooled mean but has far lower variance than the direct 5-respondent estimate.

**(d) Factor the margin of error doesn't address** : The margin of error addresses only **sampling error** 鈥?the random variation in estimates due to which 3,000 people were sampled. It does not address:

* **Non-response bias** : If Wyoming supporters/opponents of the ballot measure respond to surveys at different rates, the estimate is biased regardless of sample size
* **Undecided/late-deciding voters** : The poll may accurately capture current opinion but not voting behavior 鈥?some respondents are undecided or may change their view
* **Turnout variation** : A voter preference poll is not a turnout-weighted estimate of how people will actually vote; turnout in Wyoming can vary by party across election cycles

For Electoral College predictions, state-level margins matter. A national poll correctly estimating national opinion within 卤2% may have state-level errors of 卤6% (due to sparse state-level samples), enough to misclassify competitive states. The 2016 and 2020 polling failures were primarily state-level failures 鈥?national estimates were approximately correct 鈥?illustrating that sampling margin of error for national polls does not bound state-level prediction error.

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Response rates for telephone surveys have fallen from 80%+ in the 1990s to below 10% today. Does this mean that telephone surveys are no longer useful, or is response rate the wrong metric to focus on?

**Discussion:**

This is an active and genuinely contested question in survey methodology.

**The case that response rate is the wrong metric** :

What matters for bias is not whether people respond, but whether respondents differ from non-respondents on the survey outcome. A 10% response rate produces unbiased estimates if the 10% who respond are representative of the 100%. Conversely, a 90% response rate can be biased if the 10% who do not respond are systematically different.

Empirical evidence supports this nuance. Several studies have found that, at least for some topics, lower response rate surveys with good probability samples produce results comparable to higher response rate surveys 鈥?because non-response is approximately random with respect to the survey outcomes, or because post-stratification weighting corrects for the non-random component.

**The case for concern about response rates** :

When response rates fall very low, the space for differential non-response to operate is large. A 90% non-response rate means that the 10% who respond could be very unusual in any number of ways 鈥?not all of which can be corrected by demographic weighting. The 2020 polling failures demonstrate that even careful weighting on age, education, race, and geography can miss systematic non-response bias in political attitudes.

Moreover, as response rates fall, the cost of achieving adequate sample sizes increases. The commercial telephone survey industry has responded by using panel-based sampling (paying participants to join response panels) 鈥?which may introduce different biases (who joins paid panels?).

**The synthesis** : Response rate is a warning signal, not a guarantee of quality. Low response rates demand explicit investigation of non-response bias 鈥?comparing achieved sample demographics to population benchmarks, comparing early vs. late responders (who differ more from non-responders), and conducting systematic non-response follow-up studies. High response rates deserve less automatic trust than they historically received.

The survey methodology community has shifted toward thinking about **total survey error** 鈥?the sum of sampling error, coverage error, non-response error, and measurement error 鈥?rather than focusing on any single component. A survey can have high response rate and still be biased due to question wording or coverage. A survey can have low response rate and still provide useful estimates if non-response is well-understood and corrected.

* * *

**Q2.** The United Kingdom's 2016 Brexit referendum (Leave vs. Remain) was widely predicted by polls to be a very close contest, with most polls showing a slight Remain lead in the final days. Leave won 51.9% to 48.1%. Analyze this polling failure using the framework of total survey error.

**Discussion:**

The Brexit polling failure illustrates several of the total survey error components operating simultaneously.

**Non-response bias 鈥?differential by education and social trust** : Post-election analysis found that Leave voters were more concentrated among older, less formally educated voters in rural areas and small towns. This demographic group has lower survey response rates generally 鈥?they are harder to reach by phone or online, and less likely to participate when reached. Post-stratification on age and education helped but could not fully correct for within-cell non-response bias: within the "older, lower-education" demographic cell, Leave voters may have been systematically less likely to respond to polls than Remain voters from the same demographic group.

This is the same phenomenon as the 2016 US polling failure: demographic cells were post-stratified correctly in composition but not corrected for within-cell differential non-response by political attitude.

**Coverage issues** : UK polling used a mix of telephone and online panel surveys. Online panels over-represent more educated, politically engaged, internet-fluent respondents 鈥?who tended to be more pro-Remain. Telephone polls faced declining response rates from harder-to-reach populations. The combination produced a Remain-leaning bias in the achieved sample that demographic weighting could not fully correct.

**Measurement issues 鈥?social desirability and expressed uncertainty** : Some polling analysis suggested that Leave voters were less likely to report their true intention 鈥?either uncertain until the end, or unwilling to report a position perceived as politically incorrect in the social context of the survey. Social desirability bias in politically contentious contexts can be substantial and is not corrected by demographic weighting.

**Aggregation effects 鈥?herding** : When most polls showed a slight Remain lead, individual polling organizations faced social pressure not to publish dramatically different results. A system where multiple organizations show similar results does not provide independent confirmation if those organizations are adjusting toward each other. Aggregating correlated polls underestimates uncertainty.

**The core lesson** : The polling failures of Brexit (and 2016 US) were not primarily sampling error failures 鈥?the margin of error for individual polls was approximately 卤3%, which is technically large enough to accommodate the actual outcome. The failures were systematic biases in which the achieved samples over-represented Remain/Democratic supporters, and post-stratification on measured demographics could not correct for unmeasured attitudinal non-response bias. Total survey error was substantially larger than sampling error alone. 鈥?the sum of sampling error, coverage error, non-response error, and measurement error 鈥?rather than focusing on any single component. A survey can have high response rate and still be biased due to question wording or coverage. A survey can have low response rate and still provide useful estimates if non-response is well-understood and corrected.

### Chapter Summary

Survey methodology is the discipline of making valid inferences about populations from samples, while accounting for all the ways the sample might not represent the population.

**Probability sampling** 鈥?where every unit has a known, non-zero selection probability 鈥?is the foundation of rigorous survey inference. It enables unbiased estimation (on average) and valid uncertainty quantification.

**Stratified sampling** mirrors experimental blocking: grouping similar units together before sampling produces more efficient estimates when strata are internally homogeneous. **Cluster sampling** is used when individual-level frames are unavailable, at the cost of design effects that reduce the effective sample size.

**Non-response bias** is the dominant source of survey error in modern polling. It cannot be reduced by increasing sample size; it requires careful study design (callback protocols, mixed-mode surveys, incentives) and statistical correction (post-stratification weighting, MrP).

**The margin of error** quantifies only sampling error 鈥?the randomness of sample selection. Total survey error, which includes coverage, non-response, and measurement errors, is typically larger and often unknowable. Polling failures in 2016 and 2020 illustrate the consequences of treating margin of error as total survey uncertainty.

**Thread A** : The clinical research parallel is efficacy vs. effectiveness 鈥?trial populations are so highly selected that trial findings may not generalize to real-world patients. Pragmatic trial designs address this by deliberately sampling from the clinical population of interest.

In the next chapter, we face a different challenge: data that arrives over time, where observations are not independent of each other 鈥?and where the standard statistical toolkit fails in systematic ways.

## Chapter 25: Time Series Thinking

In 1926, the Norwegian statistician George Udny Yule published one of the most important papers in the history of statistics. He reported a disturbing finding: the annual Anglican marriage rate in England and Wales was highly correlated with the annual mortality rate from mental illness. The correlation coefficient was 0.95 鈥?extraordinarily high by any standard.

Was there something about the psychological strain of marriage that predisposed people to mental illness? Did widows and widowers die of heartbreak? Were the clergy at risk?

None of these explanations were correct. Both series had been rising over time, and two variables that both trend upward will appear correlated 鈥?even if they have nothing whatsoever to do with each other. Yule called this "nonsense correlations" or "spurious correlations," and proved mathematically that two independent random walks will appear highly correlated more often than not.

This chapter is about what happens when data arrives over time 鈥?and what goes wrong with standard statistical methods that ignore the time dimension. The short answer: quite a lot. The standard tools of regression, hypothesis testing, and confidence intervals all assume that observations are independent of each other. When data is ordered in time, yesterday's observation is the best predictor of today's observation 鈥?independence is almost never true. Ignoring this dependence leads to inflated significance, spurious correlations, and forecasts that look precise but widen dramatically as the horizon grows.

### 25.1 Autocorrelation: When the Past Predicts the Present

The most fundamental feature of time series data is **autocorrelation** : the correlation of a series with its own past values.

If today's temperature is 25掳C, tomorrow is very likely to be close to 25掳C 鈥?not because of any causal mystery, but because weather systems move slowly. Temperature is highly autocorrelated: Corr(Tt,Tt鈭?)\text{Corr}(T_t, T_{t-1})Corr(Tt鈥?Tt鈭?鈥? is close to 1. If a company's stock price is 100 USD today, tomorrow it might be 99.50 USD or 100.50 USD 鈥?prices move in small steps. Stock prices are highly autocorrelated.

#### Definition: Autocorrelation Function

The **autocorrelation function (ACF)** measures the correlation of a series {yt}\\{y_t\\}{yt鈥媫 with itself at lag kkk:

蟻k=Corr(yt,yt鈭択)=Cov(yt,yt鈭択)Var(yt)\rho_k = \text{Corr}(y_t, y_{t-k}) = \frac{\text{Cov}(y_t, y_{t-k})}{\text{Var}(y_t)}蟻k鈥?Corr(yt鈥?yt鈭択鈥?=Var(yt鈥?Cov(yt鈥?yt鈭択鈥?鈥?
The ACF at lag 0 is always 1 (a series is perfectly correlated with itself). The ACF at lag 1 measures correlation with yesterday's value. The ACF at lag kkk measures correlation with the value kkk periods ago.

A time series with no temporal dependence (pure noise) has ACF 鈮?\approx 0鈮? for all lags k>0k > 0k>0. A highly autocorrelated series has ACF that decays slowly 鈥?high correlations persist many lags into the past.

**Why autocorrelation violates standard statistical assumptions** : All of the inference machinery in Chapters 6鈥?0 assumed that observations were independently drawn. The sampling distribution of the sample mean y藟\bar{y}y藟鈥?is N(渭,蟽2/n)\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2/n)N(渭,蟽2/n) 鈥?with the 1/n1/n1/n factor arising because nnn independent observations provide nnn independent pieces of information.

With autocorrelated data, observations are not independent. The effective sample size is smaller than nnn:

neff鈮坣1+2鈭慿=1鈭炏乲n_{\text{eff}} \approx \frac{n}{1 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \rho_k}neff鈥嬧増1+2鈭慿=1鈭炩€嬒乲鈥媙鈥?
If 蟻1=0.9\rho_1 = 0.9蟻1鈥?0.9 (high autocorrelation at lag 1), the effective sample size may be only n/10n/10n/10 or less. Standard errors computed using 蟽/n\sigma/\sqrt{n}蟽/n鈥?are too small 鈥?standard tests are anti-conservative, rejecting the null too often. Confidence intervals are too narrow.

**The practical consequence** : A time series of 100 highly autocorrelated observations may contain no more independent information than 10 independent observations. Running a standard regression on time series data without accounting for autocorrelation is statistically similar to computing a confidence interval based on 10 observations but claiming it applies to 100.

### 25.2 Decomposition: Trend, Seasonality, and Residual

Most real time series contain multiple components that operate at different time scales:

**Trend** : The long-term direction of the series 鈥?upward, downward, or flat. Global temperature has an upward trend. Cassette tape sales have a downward trend.

**Seasonality** : Regular, periodic patterns that repeat at fixed intervals. Ice cream sales peak in summer. Flu hospitalizations peak in winter. Retail sales peak in December.

**Residual (irregular)** : The component remaining after trend and seasonality are removed 鈥?the part that is not systematic.

Classical decomposition expresses a time series as a combination of these components:

**Additive model** : yt=Tt+St+Rty_t = T_t + S_t + R_tyt鈥?Tt鈥?St鈥?Rt鈥?(appropriate when seasonal fluctuations are roughly constant in magnitude)

**Multiplicative model** : yt=Tt脳St脳Rty_t = T_t \times S_t \times R_tyt鈥?Tt鈥嬅桽t鈥嬅桼t鈥?(appropriate when seasonal fluctuations are proportional to the trend level)

Decomposition serves two purposes:

  1. **Understanding** : Separating trend from seasonality reveals what is actually happening. Rising hospital visits in winter may be entirely seasonal (flu season), with no underlying upward trend.
  2. **Forecasting** : Seasonal adjustment removes the predictable seasonal component, allowing better detection of non-seasonal trends and anomalies.

#### Common Misconception

A common error is to run a regression with time as a predictor and interpret the slope as a meaningful association between time and the outcome. "Sales increase by XXX per month" 鈥?is this due to a genuine time trend, or is it an artifact of unmeasured variables that are themselves trending over time? Time itself causes nothing; it is a proxy for changes in other variables. The slope of a regression on time describes the trend but cannot explain it.

### 25.3 Stationarity: The Foundation of Time Series Inference

Classical time series methods require a key assumption: **stationarity**. A time series is stationary if its statistical properties 鈥?mean, variance, and autocorrelation structure 鈥?do not change over time.

**Strictly stationary** : The joint distribution of (yt,yt+1,鈥?yt+k)(y_t, y_{t+1}, \ldots, y_{t+k})(yt鈥?yt+1鈥?鈥?yt+k鈥? is the same for all ttt.

**Weakly stationary** (covariance stationary): Mean 渭\mu渭 and variance 蟽2\sigma^2蟽2 are constant over time, and the autocorrelation Corr(yt,yt鈭択)\text{Corr}(y_t, y_{t-k})Corr(yt鈥?yt鈭択鈥? depends only on the lag kkk, not on ttt.

Most useful series are only weakly stationary (or can be made so by transformation).

**Why does stationarity matter?** In a stationary series, past observations are informative about future observations in a stable, learnable way. The relationship between yty_tyt鈥?and yt鈭?y_{t-1}yt鈭?鈥?is the same in January as in July, the same in 2010 as in 2020. We can estimate this relationship from past data and expect it to hold in the future.

In a non-stationary series, the relationship may change over time. Past patterns may not generalize to the future. Standard inference (t-tests, confidence intervals, regression) assumes stationarity and produces unreliable results when it fails.

#### The Random Walk: Non-Stationarity in Its Purest Form

The **random walk** is the canonical non-stationary process:

yt=yt鈭?+蔚t,蔚t鈭糔(0,蟽2)y_t = y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \quad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)yt鈥?yt鈭?鈥?蔚t鈥?蔚t鈥嬧埣N(0,蟽2)

Each period, the series takes a random step of random size. The variance of yty_tyt鈥?grows with ttt: Var(yt)=t蟽2\text{Var}(y_t) = t\sigma^2Var(yt鈥?=t蟽2. As ttt grows, the series can wander arbitrarily far from its starting point 鈥?a stationary series always returns to its mean, but a random walk has no fixed mean to return to.

Stock prices are approximately random walks. So is the cumulative count of goals in a soccer season, the path of a particle in Brownian motion, and (approximately) many economic time series.

**Spurious regression** : Two independent random walks will appear correlated in a regression analysis. The standard t-test on the slope will reject the null hypothesis at a rate far above 伪\alpha伪, even when the series have no true relationship. This is Yule's "nonsense correlations" 鈥?mathematically explained.

The fix: first-difference the series. Instead of regressing yty_tyt鈥?on xtx_txt鈥? regress 螖yt=yt鈭抷t鈭?\Delta y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}螖yt鈥?yt鈥嬧垝yt鈭?鈥?on 螖xt=xt鈭抶t鈭?\Delta x_t = x_t - x_{t-1}螖xt鈥?xt鈥嬧垝xt鈭?鈥? First-differencing a random walk produces an i.i.d. series (the increments), which is stationary.

### 25.4 Forecasting: Discipline at the Edge of Knowledge

Forecasting is the task of predicting future values of a time series from its past. It is one of the most practically important applications of statistics 鈥?and one of the most frequently misunderstood.

#### The Fundamental Limits of Forecasting

Time series forecasting has hard limits:

  1. **Uncertainty grows with horizon** : Forecast uncertainty (the width of prediction intervals) grows as the forecast horizon extends. For a random walk with variance 蟽2\sigma^2蟽2 per step, the hhh-step-ahead prediction interval grows as 卤z0.975蟽h\pm z_{0.975} \sigma \sqrt{h}卤z0.975鈥嬒僪鈥? A forecast 4 steps ahead is twice as uncertain as a forecast 1 step ahead. There is no method that fundamentally changes this 鈥?it is a mathematical consequence of uncertainty accumulation.

  2. **Regime changes are unpredictable** : A model trained on data from one regime cannot predict when the regime changes. The COVID-19 pandemic made models trained on pre-pandemic data useless for 2020 forecasting. Structural breaks 鈥?sudden changes in the data-generating process 鈥?are by definition not predicted by models that assume the process is stable.

  3. **Long horizons are dominated by uncertainty** : At long enough horizons, the prediction interval covers the entire plausible range of outcomes. A 30-year economic forecast is not a prediction 鈥?it is a description of scenarios. Confidence in long-horizon forecasts reflects overconfidence bias (Chapter 1) rather than statistical precision.

#### Exponential Smoothing

The simplest useful forecasting method is **exponential smoothing**. The forecast for the next period is a weighted average of the current observation and the current forecast, with the weight 伪\alpha伪 (the smoothing parameter) controlling how quickly the forecast adapts:

y^t+1=伪yt+(1鈭捨?y^t\hat{y}_{t+1} = \alpha y_t + (1-\alpha) \hat{y}_ty^鈥媡+1鈥?伪yt鈥?(1鈭捨?y^鈥媡鈥?
For 伪\alpha伪 close to 1: the forecast tracks the most recent observation closely (responsive but volatile). For 伪\alpha伪 close to 0: the forecast changes slowly (stable but slow to adapt to genuine trend changes).

Exponential smoothing weights recent observations more than older ones. Expanding the recursion shows that the forecast at time t+1t+1t+1 is a weighted average of all past observations, with weights decaying geometrically: 伪,伪(1鈭捨?,伪(1鈭捨?2,鈥alpha, \alpha(1-\alpha), \alpha(1-\alpha)^2, \ldots伪,伪(1鈭捨?,伪(1鈭捨?2,鈥?

#### AR Models: Using the Past to Predict the Future

An **autoregressive model of order ppp** (AR(ppp)) models the current value as a linear function of the previous ppp values plus noise:

yt=c+蠒1yt鈭?+蠒2yt鈭?+鈰?蠒pyt鈭抪+蔚ty_t = c + \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \phi_2 y_{t-2} + \cdots + \phi_p y_{t-p} + \varepsilon_tyt鈥?c+蠒1鈥媦t鈭?鈥?蠒2鈥媦t鈭?鈥?鈰?蠒p鈥媦t鈭抪鈥?蔚t鈥?
where ccc is a constant, 蠒i\phi_i蠒i鈥?are autoregressive coefficients, and 蔚t鈭糔(0,蟽2)\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)蔚t鈥嬧埣N(0,蟽2) is white noise (uncorrelated).

The AR(1) model is the simplest non-trivial case:

yt=c+蠒1yt鈭?+蔚ty_t = c + \phi_1 y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_tyt鈥?c+蠒1鈥媦t鈭?鈥?蔚t鈥?
If 鈭Ｏ?鈭?1|\phi_1| < 1鈭Ｏ?鈥嬧垼<1: the process is stationary 鈥?it tends to return to its mean 渭=c/(1鈭捪?)\mu = c/(1-\phi_1)渭=c/(1鈭捪?鈥?. If 蠒1=1\phi_1 = 1蠒1鈥?1: the process is a random walk (non-stationary). If 鈭Ｏ?鈭?1|\phi_1| > 1鈭Ｏ?鈥嬧垼>1: the process is explosive (rare in economics).

The ACF of an AR(1) model decays exponentially: 蟻k=蠒1k\rho_k = \phi_1^k蟻k鈥?蠒1k鈥? For 蠒1=0.8\phi_1 = 0.8蠒1鈥?0.8, 蟻1=0.8\rho_1 = 0.8蟻1鈥?0.8, 蟻2=0.64\rho_2 = 0.64蟻2鈥?0.64, 蟻10=0.810=0.107\rho_{10} = 0.8^{10} = 0.107蟻10鈥?0.810=0.107. Correlation with the past decays, but slowly.

### 25.5 Thread C: Time Series in AI

Thread C has one final installment here, connecting the time series concepts of this chapter to how AI systems process sequential data.

**Transformers and the attention mechanism** : The dominant architecture for large language models (Chapter 21) is the transformer. Unlike earlier recurrent networks (RNNs) that processed sequences one step at a time 鈥?maintaining a hidden state that summarized past tokens 鈥?transformers use **self-attention** to directly access all previous positions in the sequence.

Self-attention computes, for each position ttt, a weighted sum of all previous positions' representations, where the weights depend on the similarity between position ttt and each previous position. This is mathematically related to computing the autocorrelation function: the attention weights tell the model how much each past position should influence the current prediction.

The key statistical insight: transformers can learn long-range dependencies (high autocorrelation at large lags) that recurrent networks struggled with. This is because the direct attention path from position 100 to position 1 does not degrade with distance the way a recurrent network's hidden state does.

**Why LLMs can be inconsistent over long contexts** : Despite the attention mechanism's theoretical ability to access all past positions, in practice attention to distant past positions is often diluted. A long context (many thousands of tokens) means that each position's attention weight is spread over many candidates. The effective range of strong attention is often shorter than the theoretical maximum. This is the time series analog of effective sample size shrinkage under autocorrelation: the model nominally has access to 128,000 tokens of context, but the effective information it actively uses may be much smaller.

Additionally, LLMs trained on text data implicitly learned time series structure: the statistical patterns of how arguments develop, how topics recur, how linguistic style is maintained across a document. When the sequence is longer than the typical training examples, these implicit temporal patterns may not extrapolate well 鈥?the model's "autocorrelation model" of text may break down at lengths it was not trained to handle.

### 25.6 Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** A researcher collects monthly ice cream sales data for 5 years and runs a regression of ice cream sales on temperature. She obtains R2=0.92R^2 = 0.92R2=0.92 and p < 0.001. She concludes that temperature causes ice cream sales. What issues might be present in this analysis, and what should she have done differently?

**Answer:**

**Issue 1 鈥?Autocorrelation in the residuals** : Monthly ice cream sales are strongly autocorrelated 鈥?a high-sales month (July) tends to be followed by another high-sales month (August). Similarly, temperature is highly autocorrelated. If the researcher runs standard OLS regression without accounting for this autocorrelation, the standard errors of the regression coefficients are too small (because the effective sample size is far less than 60 monthly observations). The p < 0.001 may reflect this inflated significance rather than a strong causal signal.

She should: (a) examine the ACF of the regression residuals (if non-zero at multiple lags, autocorrelation is present), (b) use Newey-West heteroscedasticity and autocorrelation consistent (HAC) standard errors, or (c) model the autocorrelation explicitly by including lagged terms.

**Issue 2 鈥?Seasonal confounding** : Both ice cream sales and temperature have strong seasonal patterns 鈥?both peak in summer. The regression may be detecting a common seasonal pattern rather than a direct causal relationship. If the regression uses the raw series (including seasonality), it is conflating the seasonal correlation with the causal temperature effect. She should seasonally adjust both series (or control for month of year) before examining the relationship.

**Issue 3 鈥?Causal interpretation** : Even if the association is real and the autocorrelation issues are addressed, correlation does not imply causation (Chapter 18). Temperature may cause ice cream purchases via multiple mechanisms: people feel hot and want cold food, more outdoor activities occur in warm weather, etc. But the regression alone does not establish causation 鈥?it establishes association. She should acknowledge this.

**Issue 4 鈥?Spurious correlation?** : In this case, the correlation is probably genuine (temperature does predict ice cream sales). But the high R2R^2R2 and strong significance should prompt investigation rather than immediate acceptance. Running a regression on two independent trending or seasonal series will produce spurious high R2R^2R2 values 鈥?not because the series are actually related, but because both share common temporal structure.

**Q2.** Explain why two independent random walks tend to appear correlated in a regression analysis. What is the fix?

**Answer:**

**Why independent random walks appear correlated** :

A random walk yt=yt鈭?+蔚ty_t = y_{t-1} + \varepsilon_tyt鈥?yt鈭?鈥?蔚t鈥?has variance that grows with time: Var(yt)=t蟽2\text{Var}(y_t) = t\sigma^2Var(yt鈥?=t蟽2. The series has no tendency to return to any fixed mean 鈥?it wanders indefinitely. Over time, any two independent random walks will, by chance, both drift in the same direction for extended periods, creating periods of high correlation. They will also drift in opposite directions for other periods.

When we compute the regression coefficient of yty_tyt鈥?on xtx_txt鈥?(two independent random walks) and test whether it is significantly different from zero, the standard t-test is designed for i.i.d. data. For random walks, the test statistic does not follow a t-distribution 鈥?it follows a distribution with much heavier tails. The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis of no relationship, even when the series are genuinely independent, can be 70鈥?0% or more when standard tests are applied naively. This is Yule's "nonsense correlations" 鈥?the regression appears highly significant not because the series are related, but because standard inference breaks down for non-stationary series.

**The fix 鈥?first-differencing** :

Take first differences of both series: 螖yt=yt鈭抷t鈭?\Delta y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}螖yt鈥?yt鈥嬧垝yt鈭?鈥?and 螖xt=xt鈭抶t鈭?\Delta x_t = x_t - x_{t-1}螖xt鈥?xt鈥嬧垝xt鈭?鈥? For a random walk, 螖yt=蔚t\Delta y_t = \varepsilon_t螖yt鈥?蔚t鈥?鈥?pure white noise, i.i.d. and mean zero. The first-differenced series is stationary.

Regressing 螖yt\Delta y_t螖yt鈥?on 螖xt\Delta x_t螖xt鈥?tests whether changes in xxx predict changes in yyy. If the series are truly independent random walks, 螖yt\Delta y_t螖yt鈥?and 螖xt\Delta x_t螖xt鈥?will be independent, and the standard t-test will correctly have Type I error rate 伪\alpha伪.

Alternatively, if there is a genuine long-run relationship between two non-stationary series (called cointegration), first-differencing removes this long-run information. In that case, error-correction models that combine differenced and level terms are appropriate.
